citations.quote:
Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a nonempty finite state set, let each state $i$
have a nonempty finite ordered action set $A_i$, and let $c>0$. For
$a\in A_i$, choose real coefficients $q^a_{ij}$ satisfying
$$q^a_{ij}\ge0\quad(j\ne i),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}=0,$$
and a reward $r_i^a\in\mathbb R$. The row $q_i^a$ is a conservative generator
row. A deterministic policy is a map $\pi$ with $\pi(i)\in A_i$. Its policy
matrix and reward vector are
$$A^\pi_{ij}=c\,\delta_{ij}-q^{\pi(i)}_{ij},\qquad r^\pi_i=r_i^{\pi(i)}.$$
The **discounted finite-state Bellman system** is
$$cV_i-\max_{a\in A_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}V_j+r_i^a\right)=0, \qquad i\in S.$$
The policy evaluation equation for $\pi$ is $A^\pi V=r^\pi$.

Here $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

derivations.claim: Nonsingularity. Suppose $Az=0$ for a nonzero real vector $z$. The finite set $\{|z_j|:1\le j\le n\}$ has a maximum by [F3]; choose an index $i$ attaining it, so $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|>0$. By the zero row sum, $(Az)_i=cz_i+\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}(z_i-z_j)$. If $z_i>0$, every term in the sum is nonnegative and $cz_i>0$, contradicting $(Az)_i=0$. If $z_i<0$, every sum term is nonpositive and $cz_i<0$, again a contradiction. Thus the kernel is zero, and [F2] makes the square matrix nonsingular.

Inverse positivity. Let $y\ge0$ and let $z=A^{-1}y$, which exists by step 1.1. If $z_i<0$ at an index where $z$ is minimal, then $(Az)_i=cz_i+\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}(z_i-z_j)<0$, contradicting $y_i\ge0$. The finite set of coordinates of $z$ attains its minimum by [F3], so this argument proves $A^{-1}y=z\ge0$ for every $y\ge0$. Applying it to each standard basis vector shows that every entry of $A^{-1}$ is nonnegative.

Positive diagonal. Fix $i$ and set $z=A^{-1}e_i\ge0$ by step 2.1. If $z_i=0$, then $(Az)_i=\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}(0-z_j)\le0$, while $(Az)_i=(e_i)_i=1$. Hence $z_i=(A^{-1})_{ii}>0$. This proves the claim.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and integers $N_j\ge3$, $1\le j\le d$. This is the
unit-period specialization of the periodic tensor-grid definition in
[[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], with each period
$\ell_j=1$. Put
$h_j=1/N_j$ and define the periodic unit torus as
$\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$; functions on it are identified with
$\mathbb Z^d$-periodic functions on $\mathbb R^d$. The Cartesian grid has nodes
$$x_i=(i_1h_1,\ldots,i_dh_d)\pmod{\mathbb Z^d},\qquad i_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}.$$
Indices on nodal arrays are always reduced modulo $N_j$ in coordinate $j$.

For a nodal array $V=(V_i)$ and $x$ in the cell with lower corner $x_i$, write
$\widetilde x_j=(i_j+\theta_j)h_j$ in a periodic lift, where
$0\le\theta_j\le1$.
Write $I_h$ for the supplier's tensor-product multilinear interpolant. In
the local coordinates above, it is
$$I_hV(x)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^d\theta_j^{\epsilon_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-\epsilon_j}\right)V_{i+\epsilon}.$$
At cell faces either adjacent cell formula gives the same value, because the
weight of the opposite face is zero. The formula is periodic and therefore
defines $I_hV$ on $\mathbb T^d$.

In dimension two the four nodal weights on one cell are shown below. The dot is
the evaluation point; the labels are exactly the four factors in the formula.
The diagram fixes the cell convention only; no later proof relies on it.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.1]
  \draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2);
  \fill (1.2,0.8) circle (1.5pt);
  \node[below left] at (0,0) {$V_{00}$};
  \node[below right] at (3,0) {$V_{10}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,2) {$V_{01}$};
  \node[above right] at (3,2) {$V_{11}$};
  \node[below] at (1.5,-0.35) {$(1-\theta_1,\,\theta_1)$};
  \node[left] at (-0.45,1) {$(1-\theta_2,\,\theta_2)$};
  \node[above right] at (1.2,0.8) {$x$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

For the periodic tensor interpolant of [[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], every value is a convex combination of the $2^d$ corner data. Consequently nonnegative data remain nonnegative, the interpolant lies between the minimum and maximum corner values, and for any node arrays $V,W$,
$$\|\mathcal I_hV-\mathcal I_hW\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T^d_\ell)}\le\|V-W\|_{\ell^\infty}.$$
These conclusions hold at every foot, with no displacement-to-cell-size restriction.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

derivations.claim: The supplier result in [F1] says each evaluation is a convex combination of the corner data. Applying this to $W-V\ge0$ proves order preservation, and applying it to $V$ and $-V$ proves the sup-norm bound.

In one coordinate, let $x=x_i+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$ and let $L_h\phi(x)=(1-\theta)\phi(x_i)+\theta\phi(x_i+h)$. Taylor-expand both endpoints about $x$. By [F2], the linear terms cancel after weighting and $$|L_h\phi(x)-\phi(x)|\le\frac{h^2}{2}\|\phi''\|_{\infty}\bigl((1-\theta)\theta^2+\theta(1-\theta)^2\bigr)=\frac{h^2}{2}\theta(1-\theta)\|\phi''\|_{\infty}\le\frac{h^2}{8}\|\phi''\|_{\infty}.$$ This calculation also holds on the periodic seam by taking a periodic lift of the cell.

Write the tensor interpolant as the product of the one-coordinate interpolation operators $I_j$. Each $I_j$ has sup-norm at most one by step 1.1. The identity $$I_1\cdots I_d-I=\sum_{j=1}^d I_1\cdots I_{j-1}(I_j-I)$$ and the one-dimensional bound of step 1.2 give the claimed sum of errors. This proves the statement.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is
$M_K<\infty$ with $|u_\varepsilon(y)|\le M_K$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
and $y\in K$. The **upper half-relaxed limit** and the **lower half-relaxed
limit** of the family, computed in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-epsilon]]), are
$$\overline u(z):=\limsup_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \sup\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\},$$
$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and integers $N_j\ge3$, $1\le j\le d$. This is the
unit-period specialization of the periodic tensor-grid definition in
[[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], with each period
$\ell_j=1$. Put
$h_j=1/N_j$ and define the periodic unit torus as
$\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$; functions on it are identified with
$\mathbb Z^d$-periodic functions on $\mathbb R^d$. The Cartesian grid has nodes
$$x_i=(i_1h_1,\ldots,i_dh_d)\pmod{\mathbb Z^d},\qquad i_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}.$$
Indices on nodal arrays are always reduced modulo $N_j$ in coordinate $j$.

For a nodal array $V=(V_i)$ and $x$ in the cell with lower corner $x_i$, write
$\widetilde x_j=(i_j+\theta_j)h_j$ in a periodic lift, where
$0\le\theta_j\le1$.
Write $I_h$ for the supplier's tensor-product multilinear interpolant. In
the local coordinates above, it is
$$I_hV(x)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^d\theta_j^{\epsilon_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-\epsilon_j}\right)V_{i+\epsilon}.$$
At cell faces either adjacent cell formula gives the same value, because the
weight of the opposite face is zero. The formula is periodic and therefore
defines $I_hV$ on $\mathbb T^d$.

In dimension two the four nodal weights on one cell are shown below. The dot is
the evaluation point; the labels are exactly the four factors in the formula.
The diagram fixes the cell convention only; no later proof relies on it.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.1]
  \draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2);
  \fill (1.2,0.8) circle (1.5pt);
  \node[below left] at (0,0) {$V_{00}$};
  \node[below right] at (3,0) {$V_{10}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,2) {$V_{01}$};
  \node[above right] at (3,2) {$V_{11}$};
  \node[below] at (1.5,-0.35) {$(1-\theta_1,\,\theta_1)$};
  \node[left] at (-0.45,1) {$(1-\theta_2,\,\theta_2)$};
  \node[above right] at (1.2,0.8) {$x$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

For the interpolant $I_h$ of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], every cell weight is nonnegative and the weights sum to one by
[[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]. Hence
$V\le W$ on grid nodes implies $I_hV\le I_hW$, and
$\|I_hV\|_{\infty}\le\|V\|_{\infty}$. If $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ and $V_i=\phi(x_i)$, then
$$\|I_hV-\phi\|_{\infty}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2\|\partial_{jj}\phi\|_{\infty}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose a closed ball $K$ about $z_0$ contained in the open cylinder where the contact is strict. For any smaller radius $r>0$, the annulus $K\setminus B_r(z_0)$ is compact by [F3]; upper semicontinuity of $\overline V-\phi$ makes its maximum strictly less than $\overline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$. Denote the positive gap by $g_r$. The lower contact case gives the corresponding positive gap above the strict minimum.

By [F1] and [A1], select pairs $(k_m,y_m)$ with $k_m\to\infty$, $y_m\to z_0$, and $V_{k_m}(y_m)-\phi(y_m)\to \overline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$. The interpolated value $V_{k_m}(y_m)$ is a convex combination of the nodal values in its cell by [F2], so at least one cell vertex has value no smaller. Choose the first such vertex in the lexicographic order on its binary cell label $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d$, where at the first differing coordinate $0$ precedes $1$. Its spatial distance from $y_m$ is at most $\sqrt d\,h_{k_m}$; the piecewise-constant time extension has a grid time within $\tau_{k_m}$. Thus the selected nodal points converge to $z_0$. Continuity of $\phi$ makes the nodal $V-\phi$ values at least the recovery values minus a quantity tending to zero, so their lower limit is at least the upper contact value.

For all sufficiently large $m$, maximize the finite nonempty set of nodal values $U_i^n-\phi(x_i,t_n)$ inside $K$ and take its lexicographically first maximizing tuple $(i,n)$, comparing integer coordinates in displayed order and putting the smaller first differing coordinate first. A maximizer exists by [F3]; its value is at least the recovery value from step 1.2. Fix $r>0$ and let $A_r=K\setminus B_r(z_0)$. The strict gap $g_r$ from step 1.1 holds on $A_r$. For every $z\in A_r$, the set-based definition [F1] supplies a positive radius on which $V_\epsilon(y)\le\overline V(z)+g_r/8$ whenever both $\epsilon$ and $|y-z|$ are smaller than that radius. Continuity of $\phi$ and density of the positive rationals allow the following predicate on pairs $(z,q)$: $P_r(z,q)$ means $V_\epsilon(y)\le\overline V(z)+g_r/8$ for every $0<\epsilon<q$ and $|y-z|<q$, and $|\phi(y)-\phi(z)|<g_r/8$ for every $|y-z|<q$. The family $$\mathcal U_r=\{B(z,q/2):z\in A_r,\ q\in\mathbb Q_{>0},\ P_r(z,q)\}$$ is an open cover of $A_r$: for each center some real radius works by the relaxed-limit definition and continuity, and a smaller rational radius also works. This is the set of all qualifying rational pairs, not a choice of one radius for each $z$. By [F3] it has a finite subcover; let $q_*>0$ be the least radius in that finite subcover. Whenever $\epsilon<q_*$ and $y\in A_r$, a covering center gives $$V_\epsilon(y)-\phi(y)\le\overline V(z)-\phi(z)+g_r/4 \le\overline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)-3g_r/4.$$ The recovery value in step 1.2 is eventually larger than this bound, so no maximizer on the grid in $K$ lies in $A_r$. Since this holds for every $r>0$, the maximizing nodes converge to $z_0$. Their values have lower limit at least the contact value by step 1.2; the upper-limit definition [F1], applied at these nodes, gives upper limit at most the same value. Thus their values converge to the upper half-relaxed contact value.

For the lower half-relaxed limit, [F1] and [A1] select near-recovery pairs with values approaching $\underline V(z_0)$. Convex interpolation supplies a cell vertex with value no larger than the interpolated value; take the first such vertex in the binary-cell lexicographic order. Minimize over the finite grid points in $K$ and take the lexicographically first minimizer. Fix $r>0$ and use the strict lower-contact gap $g_r$ from step 1.1 on $A_r$. For each $z\in A_r$, the set-defined lower limit gives a positive radius on which $V_\epsilon(y)\ge\underline V(z)-g_r/8$ whenever both $\epsilon$ and $|y-z|$ are smaller than that radius. Define $P^-_r(z,q)$ to mean this bound holds for every $0<\epsilon<q$ and $|y-z|<q$, and $|\phi(y)-\phi(z)|<g_r/8$ for every $|y-z|<q$. The family of all $B(z,q/2)$ with $z\in A_r$, rational $q>0$, and $P^-_r(z,q)$ covers $A_r$; as in step 2.1, it uses all qualifying pairs rather than a pointwise choice. A finite subcover from [F3] has least radius $q_*>0$, so every sufficiently fine approximation at every $y\in A_r$ satisfies $$V_\epsilon(y)-\phi(y)\ge\underline V(z)-\phi(z)-g_r/4\ge\underline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)+3g_r/4.$$ The lower recovery values from the selected vertex tend to $\underline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$; hence no minimizing node lies in $A_r$ once the mesh is sufficiently fine. As this holds for each $r>0$, the minimizing nodes approach $z_0$. Their upper limit is at most the recovery contact value, while the set-defined lower limit [F1] gives lower limit at least that value, so they converge to it. This proves the dual statement.

For the finite system of [[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]],
order each finite set $A_i$ by its declared indices and put
$P=\prod_{i\in S}|A_i|$. The procedure takes a positive integer evaluation
budget $K\in\mathbb N$, $K\ge1$ (default $K=P$), and proceeds as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0(i)$ to the least-index action in $A_i$.
2. For the current policy $\pi_k$, solve exactly
   $A^{\pi_k}V^k=r^{\pi_k}$.
3. Form the strict-improvement set
   $$J_k=\left\{i:\max_{a\in A_i}(Q_i^aV^k+r_i^a)>Q_i^{\pi_k(i)}V^k+r_i^{\pi_k(i)}\right\},$$
   where $Q_i^aV=\sum_jq^a_{ij}V_j$.
4. If $J_k=\varnothing$, return $(\texttt{converged},\pi_k,V^k)$.
5. If $J_k\ne\varnothing$ and $k+1=K$, return
   $(\texttt{budget\_exhausted},\pi_k,V^k)$; this status makes no Bellman-solution
   claim.
6. Otherwise, at each $i\in J_k$ switch to the least-index maximizing action
   in $A_i$; retain $\pi_k(i)$ at every state outside $J_k$ and continue.

The policy matrix solve is well-defined by
[[lem-na-discounted-bellman-policy-matrix-inverse-positive]]. A budget of $P$
policy evaluations is sufficient by the theorem below.

For every policy $\pi$ in [[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]],
the matrix $A^\pi=cI-Q^\pi$ is nonsingular, $(A^\pi)^{-1}$ is entrywise
nonnegative, and each diagonal entry of $(A^\pi)^{-1}$ is strictly positive.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a nonempty finite state set, let each state $i$
have a nonempty finite ordered action set $A_i$, and let $c>0$. For
$a\in A_i$, choose real coefficients $q^a_{ij}$ satisfying
$$q^a_{ij}\ge0\quad(j\ne i),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}=0,$$
and a reward $r_i^a\in\mathbb R$. The row $q_i^a$ is a conservative generator
row. A deterministic policy is a map $\pi$ with $\pi(i)\in A_i$. Its policy
matrix and reward vector are
$$A^\pi_{ij}=c\,\delta_{ij}-q^{\pi(i)}_{ij},\qquad r^\pi_i=r_i^{\pi(i)}.$$
The **discounted finite-state Bellman system** is
$$cV_i-\max_{a\in A_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}V_j+r_i^a\right)=0, \qquad i\in S.$$
The policy evaluation equation for $\pi$ is $A^\pi V=r^\pi$.

Here $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

derivations.claim: Let $\pi_{k+1}$ follow a strict-improvement step from $\pi_k$. At an unchanged state $i$, $\pi_{k+1}(i)=\pi_k(i)$, so $(r^{\pi_{k+1}}-A^{\pi_{k+1}}V^k)_i=0$ by [F1]. At a switched state $i$, the new action has $\sum_jq^{\pi_{k+1}(i)}_{ij}V_j^k+r_i^{\pi_{k+1}(i)}>cV_i^k$, while the old policy equation gives $\sum_jq^{\pi_k(i)}_{ij}V_j^k+r_i^{\pi_k(i)}=cV_i^k$. Therefore the vector $z=r^{\pi_{k+1}}-A^{\pi_{k+1}}V^k$ is nonnegative and is strictly positive at every switched state.

The new exact policy solve gives $$A^{\pi_{k+1}}(V^{k+1}-V^k)=r^{\pi_{k+1}}-A^{\pi_{k+1}}V^k=z.$$ Multiplying by the nonnegative inverse in [F2] yields $V^{k+1}-V^k=(A^{\pi_{k+1}})^{-1}z\ge0$. At a switched state $i$, the $i$th coordinate is at least $(A^{\pi_{k+1}})^{-1}_{ii}z_i>0$, so the value increase is strict there.

If a policy recurred after at least one strict switch, exact evaluation of that same nonsingular policy matrix would reproduce its unique value vector, contradicting the componentwise nondecrease and the strict increase at each intervening switch from step 2.1. Thus all evaluated policies are distinct. There are only $P$ policies by [F3], so after at most $P$ evaluations the strict-improvement set is empty; the budget-$P$ algorithm cannot exhaust first.

At termination, no action row exceeds the current policy row at any state. The policy equation says that the current row equals $cV_i$; hence $cV_i=\max_a(\sum_jq^a_{ij}V_j+r_i^a)$ at every state, so $V$ solves the Bellman system. For uniqueness, suppose $V,W$ are two solutions and let $d=V-W$. Choose a state $i$ where $d_i=\max_jd_j$, which exists by [F3]. For every action, $$\sum_jq^a_{ij}d_j=\sum_{j\ne i}q^a_{ij}(d_j-d_i)\le0$$ by the generator signs and row sum. The difference of the two maxima is at most the maximum of the rowwise differences, so $cd_i\le\max_a\sum_jq^a_{ij}d_j\le0$, whence $d_i\le0$. Thus $\max_j(V_j-W_j)\le0$. Interchanging $V,W$ gives the reverse inequality, so $V=W$.

Use the model of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] and a periodic grid with integers $N_j\ge3$, $h_j=1/N_j$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. For a nodal array $V$, define
$$D_{jj}^hV_i=\frac{V_{i+e_j}-2V_i+V_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$
For a control $a$, define
$$D_{j,a}^{up}V_i=\begin{cases}(V_i-V_{i-e_j})/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)\ge0,\\(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)<0.\end{cases}$$
The recurrence is
$$U_i^{n+1}=U_i^n+\tau\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^d\left[\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{jj}^hU_i+b_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{j,a}^{up}U_i\right]+f^a(x_i,t_n)\right\}.$$
At each time level $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, admit the update only when, at every node, control, and coordinate,
$$|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\le\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n),$$
and
$$\tau\max_{i,a}\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)}{h_j^2}+\frac{|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\right)\le1.$$
Initialize by $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, evaluating coefficients at $(x_i,t_n)$. Return $U^M$. No claim about an arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is included.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

$h_j=1/N_j$ and define the periodic unit torus as
$\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$; functions on it are identified with

derivations.claim: Fix one control row and abbreviate $\alpha=\alpha_j^a$, $b=b_j^a$, $h=h_j$. If $b\ge0$, the two neighbor transition weights in coordinate $j$ are $\tau(\alpha/h^2-b/h)$ at $x_i-h e_j$ and $\tau\alpha/h^2$ at $x_i+h e_j$. If $b<0$, they are $\tau\alpha/h^2$ at $x_i-h e_j$ and $\tau(\alpha/h^2-|b|/h)$ at $x_i+h e_j$. Their sum is $\tau(2\alpha/h^2-|b|/h)$ and their signed first moment is $\tau b$. The diffusion-dominance inequality in [F1] makes both neighbor coefficients nonnegative. The center coefficient is $1-\tau\sum_j(2\alpha_j^a/h_j^2-|b_j^a|/h_j)$, which is nonnegative by the CFL inequality in [F1]. Including the center, the row weights sum to one. Summing over coordinates gives mean displacement $\tau b^a(x_i,t_n)$. The raw squared displacement is at most $$\tau\sum_j\left(2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)-|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\right) \le2\tau dA_*.$$ Subtracting the squared mean cannot increase the second moment.

Unroll $n_k$ updates as a finite transition tree. At a node of the tree, the maximum in the scheme chooses one of finitely many control rows; that row is a finite probability distribution by step 1.1. The terminal value is thus a maximum of finite weighted averages of $u_0(X_{n_k})$ plus accumulated rewards. On every branch the sum of the drift means has magnitude at most $Bt_k$. The centered increments have conditional weighted mean zero. For two different times, the weighted cross term vanishes by first summing the later centered increment over all branches extending a fixed earlier path prefix. Expanding the square and using step 1.1 gives, uniformly over all finite policies, $$\mathbb E|X_{n_k}-x_i|^2\le2B^2t_k^2+4dA_*t_k.$$ The accumulated reward has magnitude at most $Ft_k$.

Put $M_0=\|u_0\|_\infty$. For any $0<\delta<1$, split each finite endpoint average according to $|X_{n_k}-x_i|\le\delta$. On that part the change in $u_0$ is at most $\omega_0(\delta)$ by [F3]; on the complement it is at most $2M_0$. The complement weight is at most $\mathbb E|X_{n_k}-x_i|^2/\delta^2$. Therefore every policy average differs from $u_0(x_i)$ by at most $$\omega_0(\delta)+\frac{2M_0}{\delta^2} \left(2B^2t_k^2+4dA_*t_k\right)+Ft_k.$$ This bound is independent of $i$ and of the policy; taking a finite maximum preserves it. First let $k\to\infty$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$ to obtain the claimed uniform initial trace.

Use the model of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] and a periodic grid with integers $N_j\ge3$, $h_j=1/N_j$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. For a nodal array $V$, define
$$D_{jj}^hV_i=\frac{V_{i+e_j}-2V_i+V_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$
For a control $a$, define
$$D_{j,a}^{up}V_i=\begin{cases}(V_i-V_{i-e_j})/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)\ge0,\\(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)<0.\end{cases}$$
The recurrence is
$$U_i^{n+1}=U_i^n+\tau\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^d\left[\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{jj}^hU_i+b_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{j,a}^{up}U_i\right]+f^a(x_i,t_n)\right\}.$$
At each time level $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, admit the update only when, at every node, control, and coordinate,
$$|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\le\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n),$$
and
$$\tau\max_{i,a}\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)}{h_j^2}+\frac{|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\right)\le1.$$
Initialize by $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, evaluating coefficients at $(x_i,t_n)$. Return $U^M$. No claim about an arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is included.

derivations.claim: Fix $i,a,j$ and abbreviate $\alpha=\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)$, $b=b_j^a(x_i,t_n)$, and $h=h_j$. If $b\ge0$, the coefficient of $U_{i-e_j}$ in the update is $\tau(\alpha/h^2-b/h)$ and that of $U_{i+e_j}$ is $\tau\alpha/h^2$. If $b<0$, the coefficient of $U_{i+e_j}$ is $\tau(\alpha/h^2-|b|/h)$ and that of $U_{i-e_j}$ is $\tau\alpha/h^2$. Each is nonnegative by $|b|h\le\alpha$ in [F1].

The center coefficient is $$1-\tau\sum_j\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a}{h_j^2}-\frac{|b_j^a|}{h_j}\right).$$ It is at least $1-\tau\sum_j(2\alpha_j^a/h_j^2+|b_j^a|/h_j)\ge0$ by [F1]. For each coordinate, the two neighbor coefficients sum to $\tau(2\alpha_j^a/h_j^2-|b_j^a|/h_j)$; adding the center coefficient therefore gives one. Hence each fixed-control update is a convex combination plus its constant forcing.
A convex combination is order-preserving in its nodal inputs. The maximum of finitely many order-preserving control maps is order-preserving, proving the claim.

unit-period specialization of the periodic tensor-grid definition in
[[def-semilagrangian-periodic-grid-and-interpolant]], with each period
$\ell_j=1$. Put
$h_j=1/N_j$ and define the periodic unit torus as
$\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$; functions on it are identified with
$\mathbb Z^d$-periodic functions on $\mathbb R^d$. The Cartesian grid has nodes
$$x_i=(i_1h_1,\ldots,i_dh_d)\pmod{\mathbb Z^d},\qquad i_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}.$$
Indices on nodal arrays are always reduced modulo $N_j$ in coordinate $j$.

For a nodal array $V=(V_i)$ and $x$ in the cell with lower corner $x_i$, write
$\widetilde x_j=(i_j+\theta_j)h_j$ in a periodic lift, where
$0\le\theta_j\le1$.
Write $I_h$ for the supplier's tensor-product multilinear interpolant. In
the local coordinates above, it is
$$I_hV(x)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^d\theta_j^{\epsilon_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-\epsilon_j}\right)V_{i+\epsilon}.$$
At cell faces either adjacent cell formula gives the same value, because the
weight of the opposite face is zero. The formula is periodic and therefore
defines $I_hV$ on $\mathbb T^d$.

In dimension two the four nodal weights on one cell are shown below. The dot is
the evaluation point; the labels are exactly the four factors in the formula.
The diagram fixes the cell convention only; no later proof relies on it.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.1]
  \draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2);
  \fill (1.2,0.8) circle (1.5pt);
  \node[below left] at (0,0) {$V_{00}$};
  \node[below right] at (3,0) {$V_{10}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,2) {$V_{01}$};
  \node[above right] at (3,2) {$V_{11}$};

  \node[left] at (-0.45,1) {$(1-\theta_2,\,\theta_2)$};
  \node[above right] at (1.2,0.8) {$x$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

For the interpolant $I_h$ of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], every cell weight is nonnegative and the weights sum to one by
[[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]. Hence
$V\le W$ on grid nodes implies $I_hV\le I_hW$, and
$\|I_hV\|_{\infty}\le\|V\|_{\infty}$. If $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ and $V_i=\phi(x_i)$, then
$$\|I_hV-\phi\|_{\infty}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2\|\partial_{jj}\phi\|_{\infty}.$$

Use the model and coefficient notation of [[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]] and the periodic grid of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]]. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. Choose a finite nonempty control set $A_k\subseteq A$. For a finite control model take $A_k=A$; for compact controls use a sequence of finite nonempty sets with the stated uniform Hamiltonian error. For each control and grid node put
$$b_{a,j}^+=\max\{b_{a,j},0\},\qquad b_{a,j}^- =\max\{-b_{a,j},0\},$$
and define the explicit row
$$G^a_i(V)=V_i+\tau\left[\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{b_{a,j}^+(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)+\frac{b_{a,j}^-(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i-e_j}-V_i)\right)+\ell_a(x_i,t_n)\right].$$
The periodic HJB upwind update at time $t_n$ is
$$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}G_i^a(U^n).$$
At every step $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, require the CFL condition
$$\tau\max_{a,i}\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{|b_{a,j}(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\le1$$
Initialize $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$. Return $U^M$. Since the transport velocity in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] is $-b_a$ for this Hamiltonian sign convention, the displayed one-sided direction is its sign-reflected upwind row.

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. Whenever the controls are
discretized, use a sequence of finite nonempty sets $A_k\subseteq A$ and define
$$H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Define the Hamiltonian error by
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|.$$
The sequence is admissible when $\eta_k(R)\to0$ for every $R<\infty$.
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and

([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

derivations.claim: For a semi-Lagrangian row at a node $x_i$ and action $a$, view its interpolation weights as a finite probability vector on the cell nodes around $y=x_i+\tau b_a(x_i,t)$. In a periodic lift, the weighted mean of each coordinate is $(1-\theta_j)x_{i_j}+\theta_j(x_{i_j}+h_j)=y_j$, by the product formula in [F1]. The centered interpolation error $\xi$ therefore has weighted mean zero and satisfies $|\xi|^2\le\sum_jh_j^2$.

For an upwind row, the weights in [F2] are nonnegative and sum to one by CFL. The weighted mean displacement to the previous-time node is $\tau b_a$: in coordinate $j$ it is $\tau(b_j^+/h_j)h_j-\tau(b_j^-/h_j)h_j=\tau b_j$. Its centered error $\xi$ has mean zero and second moment at most $\tau\sum_j|b_j|h_j\le\tau B\sum_jh_j$, since subtracting the squared mean cannot increase the second moment.

Unroll either update for the finite number $n$ of steps. At each stage the minimum chooses one of finitely many control rows, and each row is a finite weighted average; induction therefore represents the value as the minimum of finite weighted path costs $u_0(X_n)+\sum_{r<n}\tau\ell_r$. Along any such controlled path the sum of the drift increments has norm at most $Bt$. The centered increments have conditional mean zero. For $r<s$, summing the increment $\xi_s$ over all next-branch weights from each fixed path prefix through time $s-1$ gives zero; hence the finite weighted cross term $\mathbb E(\xi_r\cdot\xi_s)$ is zero. Expanding the square therefore shows that their total second moment is at most $n\sum_jh_j^2$ for the semi-Lagrangian rows and $tB\sum_jh_j$ for the upwind rows. Thus the endpoint displacement obeys $$\mathbb E|X_n-x_i|^2\le2B^2t^2+2n\sum_jh_j^2$$ for the semi-Lagrangian case and $$\mathbb E|X_n-x_i|^2\le2B^2t^2+2tB\sum_jh_j$$ for the upwind case. Every path's accumulated reward has magnitude at most $Lt$.

Let $M_0=\|u_0\|_\infty$ and let $\omega_0(\delta)\to0$ be the uniform modulus from [F4]. For any $0<\delta<1$, split the finite weighted endpoint average into paths with $|X_n-x_i|\le\delta$ and its complement. On the first set, $|u_0(X_n)-u_0(x_i)|\le\omega_0(\delta)$; on the complement, it is at most $2M_0$. The complement weight is at most $\mathbb E|X_n-x_i|^2/\delta^2$. By step 1.3 this tends to zero as $t_n\to0$ under $h_{\max}^2/\tau\to0$ for the semi-Lagrangian scheme, and under $h_{\max}\to0$ for the upwind scheme. The reward contributes at most $Lt_n$; the same two-sided bound holds after taking a minimum over policies. First let the mesh and $t_n$ tend to zero, then let $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the asserted uniform initial trace.

citations.quote: Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. Whenever the controls are
discretized, use a sequence of finite nonempty sets $A_k\subseteq A$ and define
$$H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Define the Hamiltonian error by
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|.$$
The sequence is admissible when $\eta_k(R)\to0$ for every $R<\infty$.
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

Let $u$ be upper semicontinuous and $v$ lower semicontinuous on the periodic
space-time cylinder. A **second-order parabolic viscosity subsolution** of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] is a function $u$
such that every $C^{1,2}$ test function $\phi$ for which $u-\phi$ has a local
maximum at $(x_0,t_0)$, $0<t_0<T$, satisfies
$$\phi_t(x_0,t_0)-\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_j\left(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j}\right)(x_0,t_0)+f^a(x_0,t_0)\right\}\le0.$$
Here $C^{1,2}$ means that $\phi_t$, all first spatial derivatives, and all
second spatial derivatives exist and are continuous near the contact point.
A **supersolution** is lower semicontinuous and satisfies the reverse
inequality at every local minimum. A viscosity solution is both. For the Cauchy
problem, the relaxed initial conditions are
$$\limsup_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}u(y,s)\le u_0(x),\qquad \liminf_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}v(y,s)\ge u_0(x).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

derivations.claim: Start with an upper contact at $z_0=(x_0,t_0)$ for a $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$ test $\phi$. On a closed Euclidean space-time ball $K$ contained in the interior cylinder, define $\widetilde\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. The added term and all derivatives relevant to the chosen test class vanish at $z_0$, while $u-\widetilde\phi$ is strictly smaller than $u(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$ at every other point of the contact neighborhood. Thus the original and strictified tests have the same PDE residual at $z_0$.

Choose a nonnegative unit-mass mollifier $\rho_\delta$ supported in the ball of radius $\delta$ from [F1], with $\delta$ small enough that its convolution samples only points in the contact neighborhood. Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of $K$ and supported inside that contact neighborhood using [F1], multiply $\widetilde\phi$ by it, and extend the product by zero. Convolve this compactly supported function with $\rho_\delta$ to obtain $\phi_\delta$. Rewriting the convolution with the smooth kernel as $\int g(y)\rho_\delta(z-y)\,dy$ shows by uniform difference quotients on the compact support that $\phi_\delta$ is $C^\infty$. On $K$ it coincides with convolution of $\widetilde\phi$ alone. For a $C^1$ function $g$, [F5] gives $$\frac{g(z+h e_j)-g(z)}h=\int_0^1\partial_jg(z+\theta h e_j)\,d\theta$$ when the indicated derivative exists. Uniform continuity of $\partial_jg$ on the compact neighborhood makes these difference quotients converge uniformly as $h\to0$. Integrating this uniform limit against $\rho_\delta$ proves $\partial_j(\rho_\delta*g)=\rho_\delta*\partial_jg$. For a second spatial derivative, apply this identity first to $g=\widetilde\phi$ and then to $g=\partial_j\widetilde\phi$; this uses only the continuous second derivative, not a third derivative. Apply it once for time and once for each first spatial derivative. Thus $D^\alpha\phi_\delta= \rho_\delta*D^\alpha\widetilde\phi$ for exactly the derivatives required in the $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$ class. By [F2], $$\sup_{z\in K'}|D^\alpha\phi_\delta(z)-D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z)| \le\sup_{z\in K',\ |y|\le\delta}|D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z-y)-D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z)|\longrightarrow0$$ on each smaller compact ball $K'$. Hence the approximants converge in $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$, respectively.

The upper semicontinuous function $u-\phi_\delta$ attains a maximum on $K$ by [F3]. The strict gap from step 1.1 and uniform convergence from the preceding approximation step imply that, for every fixed neighborhood of $z_0$, all maximizing points lie in that neighborhood once $\delta$ is sufficiently small; the boundary of $K$ is excluded for the same reason. At any such maximizing point $z_\delta$, adding the constant $u(z_\delta)-\phi_\delta(z_\delta)$ makes $\phi_\delta$ a smooth upper test. Apply the assumed smooth-test inequality there.

The maximizing points in step 3.1 approach $z_0$ uniformly over the maximizing set, and the required derivatives of $\phi_\delta$ converge uniformly to those of $\widetilde\phi$ on $K'$ by step 2.1. Continuity of the PDE residual [F4] therefore lets the smooth-test inequalities pass to the residual of $\widetilde\phi$ at $z_0$, which equals that of $\phi$ by step 1.1. This proves the upper-test implication. For a lower contact, replace maxima by minima and reverse the inequalities; the same uniform gap and derivative convergence apply. Since smooth tests are themselves in both larger test classes, the reverse implications are immediate.

Use the model of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] and a periodic grid with integers $N_j\ge3$, $h_j=1/N_j$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. For a nodal array $V$, define
$$D_{jj}^hV_i=\frac{V_{i+e_j}-2V_i+V_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$
For a control $a$, define
$$D_{j,a}^{up}V_i=\begin{cases}(V_i-V_{i-e_j})/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)\ge0,\\(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)<0.\end{cases}$$
The recurrence is
$$U_i^{n+1}=U_i^n+\tau\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^d\left[\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{jj}^hU_i+b_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{j,a}^{up}U_i\right]+f^a(x_i,t_n)\right\}.$$
At each time level $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, admit the update only when, at every node, control, and coordinate,
$$|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\le\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n),$$
and
$$\tau\max_{i,a}\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)}{h_j^2}+\frac{|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\right)\le1.$$
Initialize by $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, evaluating coefficients at $(x_i,t_n)$. Return $U^M$. No claim about an arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is included.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

derivations.claim: Applying [F2] at $x_i\pm h_je_j$ and cancelling the odd terms gives $$D_{jj}^h\phi(x_i,t_n)=\phi_{x_jx_j}(x_i,t_n)+O(h_j^2\|\phi_{x_j^4}\|_\infty).$$ Applying [F2] to the one-sided difference in [F1] gives $$D_{j,a}^{up}\phi(x_i,t_n)=\phi_{x_j}(x_i,t_n)+O(h_j\|\phi_{x_jx_j}\|_\infty)$$ for either sign of $b_j^a$. The coefficient bounds make these estimates uniform over the finite action and coordinate sets.

Taylor expansion in time gives $$\frac{\phi(x_i,t_n+\tau)-\phi(x_i,t_n)}{\tau} =\phi_t(x_i,t_n)+O(\tau\|\phi_{tt}\|_\infty).$$ Substitute the spatial estimates of step 1.1 into the update in [F1]. Since $|\max_a X_a-\max_aY_a|\le\max_a|X_a-Y_a|$, the uniform spatial residual is bounded by the sum displayed in the statement. Combining with the time estimate gives its formula and its explicit smoothness dependence.

The mesh consistency residual tends to zero when $\tau\to0$ and $h_{\max}\to0$ with bounded coefficients. It supplies the local consistency input for the half-relaxed-limit result and makes no assertion of a universal convergence rate.

Choose integers $N_j\ge3$, a number $M\ge1$ of time steps, and
$\tau=T/M$. Sample $u_0$ at the grid nodes of
[[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]] and set
$U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$. At each $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, compute
$$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}\left\{ I_hU^n\bigl(x_i+\tau b_a(x_i,t_n)\bigr)+\tau\ell_a(x_i,t_n) \right\},\qquad t_n=n\tau.$$
The position is evaluated on the torus, so its coordinates wrap modulo one.
The algorithm always uses a finite nonempty set $A_k\subset A$. For a finite
control model take $A_k=A$; for a compact control model, supply finite sets
whose Hamiltonian errors $\eta_k(R)$ from
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]] tend to zero on every bounded
momentum set. This is the declared finite-control approximation branch; it
does not presume an unimplemented continuous minimization oracle. Return
$U^M$.

The update is the explicit Euler-footpoint semi-Lagrangian branch specified by
the plan. It defines its footpoint and interpolant locally; no unauthored
characteristic-flow estimate is presumed.

For the interpolant $I_h$ of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], every cell weight is nonnegative and the weights sum to one by
[[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]. Hence
$V\le W$ on grid nodes implies $I_hV\le I_hW$, and
$\|I_hV\|_{\infty}\le\|V\|_{\infty}$. If $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ and $V_i=\phi(x_i)$, then
$$\|I_hV-\phi\|_{\infty}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2\|\partial_{jj}\phi\|_{\infty}.$$

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. Whenever the controls are
discretized, use a sequence of finite nonempty sets $A_k\subseteq A$ and define
$$H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Define the Hamiltonian error by
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|.$$
The sequence is admissible when $\eta_k(R)\to0$ for every $R<\infty$.

uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

Let $y_a=x_i+\tau b_a(x_i,t_n)$ in a periodic lift. $$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}G_i^a(U^n).$$

derivations.claim: The CFL condition makes the center coefficient in [F1] nonnegative; all neighbor coefficients are nonnegative by $b_{a,j}^\pm\ge0$. Their sum is $$1-\tau\sum_j|b_{a,j}|/h_j+\tau\sum_j(b_{a,j}^++b_{a,j}^-)/h_j=1.$$ Thus each row is a convex combination of nodal values plus $\tau\ell_a$ and is order-preserving. A pointwise minimum of order-preserving maps is order-preserving. Every row value lies in $[-\|U^n\|_\infty-\tau L,\|U^n\|_\infty+\tau L]$, so the minimum has the same bound.

If $b_{a,j}\ge0$, the drift term in [F1] is $b_{a,j}(\phi(x_i+h_je_j)-\phi(x_i))/h_j$; if $b_{a,j}<0$, it is $b_{a,j}(\phi(x_i)-\phi(x_i-h_je_j))/h_j$. In either case it equals $b_{a,j}\phi_{x_j}(x_i)+O(|b_{a,j}|h_j\|\phi_{x_jx_j}\|_\infty)$ by [F2]. The time increment divided by $\tau$ is $\phi_t(x_i,t_n)+O(\tau\|\phi_{tt}\|_\infty)$. The minimum is Lipschitz with respect to uniform perturbations of its entries, and replacing $A$ by $A_k$ changes the Hamiltonian by at most $\eta_k(P)$. Combining these estimates and [F3] gives the stated residual.
The weights in [F1] show that the upwind step is a monotone, stable, consistent approximation with the stated error. This conclusion is local consistency only and asserts no solution-error rate.

Under the two inequalities in [[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]],
every fixed-control row of its explicit update is an affine combination of the
center and the two coordinate neighbors with nonnegative coefficients summing
to one, plus $\tau f^a$. Therefore the max over controls is order-preserving.

Use the model of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] and a periodic grid with integers $N_j\ge3$, $h_j=1/N_j$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. For a nodal array $V$, define
$$D_{jj}^hV_i=\frac{V_{i+e_j}-2V_i+V_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$
For a control $a$, define
$$D_{j,a}^{up}V_i=\begin{cases}(V_i-V_{i-e_j})/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)\ge0,\\(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)<0.\end{cases}$$
The recurrence is
$$U_i^{n+1}=U_i^n+\tau\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^d\left[\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{jj}^hU_i+b_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{j,a}^{up}U_i\right]+f^a(x_i,t_n)\right\}.$$
At each time level $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, admit the update only when, at every node, control, and coordinate,
$$|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\le\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n),$$
and
$$\tau\max_{i,a}\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)}{h_j^2}+\frac{|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\right)\le1.$$
Initialize by $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, evaluating coefficients at $(x_i,t_n)$. Return $U^M$. No claim about an arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is included.

Assume the coefficients are bounded and periodic and a periodic test function
$\phi$ is smooth with bounded derivatives $\phi_{tt}$, $\phi_{x_jx_j}$, and
$\phi_{x_jx_jx_jx_j}$, and the coefficients are bounded. For the scheme of
[[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]], define the normalized
local residual
$$R_{h,\tau}(x_i,t_n)=\frac{\phi(x_i,t_n+\tau)-S_{h,\tau}\phi(\cdot,t_n)_i}{\tau}.$$
Then
$$R_{h,\tau}=\phi_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j})+f^a\right\} +O\left(\tau+\max_j\left[\alpha_{j,\max}h_j^2\|\phi_{x_j^4}\|_\infty+ |b_j|_{\max}h_j\|\phi_{x_jx_j}\|_\infty\right]\right),$$
where $\alpha_{j,\max}:=\sup_{a,x,t}\alpha_j^a(x,t)$ and
$|b_j|_{\max}:=\sup_{a,x,t}|b_j^a(x,t)|$. The bound is uniform over nodes and
times before the terminal step. The $O(\cdot)$ is a
smooth-test residual estimate, not a solution-error rate.

Let $V_k$ be locally bounded periodic interpolant extensions of finite nodal
arrays on grids with $h_k\to0$ and time steps $\tau_k\to0$. Regard this
sequence as the family $V_\epsilon=V_k$ when
$(k+1)^{-1}<\epsilon\le k^{-1}$, and form its upper and lower half-relaxed
limits as in
[[def-half-relaxed-limits]]. If $\overline V-\phi$ has a strict local maximum
at an interior point $z_0=(x_0,t_0)$ for a smooth test $\phi$, then there are
mesh indices $k_m\to\infty$ and grid points $z_m=(x_{i_m},t_{n_m})\to z_0$
such that $V_{k_m}(z_m)-\phi(z_m)\to\overline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$ and $z_m$ is
a local maximum of the corresponding nodal values minus $\phi$ on a fixed
closed space-time ball. The lower half-relaxed limit has the dual strict
minimum property. The proof uses Countable Choice only for sequential recovery
from the set-defined half-relaxed limit.

For the continuous first-order Hamiltonian of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]], requiring the subsolution or
supersolution inequality only for smooth ($C^\infty$) local test functions is
equivalent to requiring it for all $C^1$ tests. For the diagonal second-order
operator of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], the
same equivalence holds between smooth tests and all $C^{1,2}$ tests in
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]]. The result is local in
space-time and applies to upper semicontinuous subsolutions and lower
semicontinuous supersolutions.

Let $u_0$ be continuous and periodic, and use the explicit diagonal-diffusion
scheme of [[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]] with mesh
widths $h_{k,j}\to0$, time steps $\tau_k\to0$, and its diffusion-dominance
and CFL inequalities at every row. Then for every sequence of integers
$n_k\ge0$ with $t_k=n_k\tau_k\to0$ and $t_k$ within the computed horizon,
$$\sup_i|U_i^{n_k}-u_0(x_i)|\longrightarrow0.$$
The estimate is uniform over all finite control choices generated by the
maximization in the scheme.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is
$M_K<\infty$ with $|u_\varepsilon(y)|\le M_K$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
and $y\in K$. The **upper half-relaxed limit** and the **lower half-relaxed
limit** of the family, computed in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-epsilon]]), are
$$\overline u(z):=\limsup_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \sup\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\},$$
$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The row weights in [F1] give $$\|U_k^n\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty+n\tau_kF \le\|u_0\|_\infty+TF.$$ Multilinear interpolation is a convex combination, so the same bound holds for the space-time extensions. They are locally bounded and their half-relaxed limits have the semicontinuity and order properties in [F6].

Let $\overline U-\phi$ have a local maximum at $(x_0,t_0)$, with $0<t_0<T$ and smooth $\phi$. Add $\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ to $\phi$; this makes the contact strict without changing its derivatives used by the PDE at $(x_0,t_0)$, as in [F4]. Select nodal local maxima $(x_k,t_k)$ from [F3] and put $c_k=U_{i_k}^{n_k}-\phi(x_k,t_k)$. All coordinate neighbors used by the explicit stencil at the previous time lie in the fixed contact cylinder for sufficiently large $k$, because their distance to $(x_k,t_k)$ is at most $h_{k,\max}+\tau_k$. Thus $U_j^{n_k-1}\le\phi(x_j,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k$ at every stencil node. Monotonicity and shift invariance in [F1] give $$U_{i_k}^{n_k}=S_k(U^{n_k-1})_{i_k} \le S_k(\phi(\cdot,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k)_{i_k} =S_k(\phi(\cdot,t_k-\tau_k))_{i_k}+c_k.$$ At the contact node $U_{i_k}^{n_k}=\phi(x_k,t_k)+c_k$, so the normalized residual is nonpositive. Passing to the limit by [F2] yields $$\phi_t-\max_a\{\sum_j(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j})+f^a\}\le0$$ at $(x_0,t_0)$.

At a local minimum of $\underline U-\phi$, subtract $\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ from $\phi$ to make the contact strict without changing its tested derivatives, as in [F4]. The minimizing nodes in [F3] give $U_j^{n_k-1}\ge\phi(x_j,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k$ on the stencil. Order preservation reverses the update inequality, so the residual is nonnegative and its limit gives the supersolution inequality. By [F4], both inequalities extend from smooth tests to all tests in the declared $C^{1,2}$ class.

The initial-trace estimate [F5] and uniform continuity of $u_0$ show that every space-time sequence with mesh tending to zero and time tending to zero has values tending to $u_0$ at its limiting spatial point; the spatial interpolation adds at most the modulus of $u_0$ at distance $\sqrt d\,h_{k,\max}$. Therefore the upper and lower relaxed limits both have the prescribed relaxed initial trace. Boundedness and semicontinuity were proved in step 1.1, completing the stability statement.
