risk_review.notes: All four steps checked with the completed monotonicity, smooth consistency, contact, smooth-test and initial-trace suppliers. Finite convex rows give ||U^n||≤||u0||+TF. At upper contacts all previous-time stencil nodes eventually lie in the fixed contact ball, so monotonicity plus constant shifts gives a nonpositive normalized residual; lower contacts reverse the inequality. Quartic strictification preserves the tested derivatives and the smooth-test lemma extends to C1,2. The trace lemma plus interpolation modulus covers joint approach to t=0, including the constant negative-time extension. Countable Choice is charged only for contact recovery. No equality of envelopes or comparison is smuggled into this stability theorem.

citations.quote:
For the update $S_{h,\tau}$ of
[[alg-na-positive-interpolation-semilagrangian-hjb-step]], if $V\le W$ at all
nodes then $S_{h,\tau}V\le S_{h,\tau}W$. If $|\ell_a|\le L$, then
$$\|S_{h,\tau}V\|_\infty\le\|V\|_\infty+\tau L.$$
For $\phi\in C^2$ in space and time with bounded derivatives, on a compact
test region with $|D\phi|\le P$,
$$\frac{\phi(t_n+\tau,x_i)-S_{h,\tau}\phi(t_n,\cdot)_i}{\tau} =\phi_t(x_i,t_n)+H(x_i,t_n,D\phi(x_i,t_n)) +O\left(\tau+\frac{h_{\max}^2}{\tau}+\eta_k(P)\right).$$
The term $\eta_k(P)$ is zero when the full finite control set is used.

Assume the first-order HJB coefficients satisfy the hypotheses of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]]. Under the CFL condition in
[[alg-na-upwind-hjb-grid-step]], each one-control update is a convex
combination of the current node and its one-sided neighbors plus
$\tau\ell_a$. Consequently the control-minimum update is order-preserving and
$$\|U^{n+1}\|_\infty\le\|U^n\|_\infty+\tau L.$$
For a smooth periodic test function $\phi$ with bounded derivatives through
order two, the normalized local residual satisfies
$$\frac{\phi(t_n+\tau,x_i)-S_{h,\tau}\phi(t_n,\cdot)_i}{\tau} =\phi_t(x_i,t_n)+H(x_i,t_n,D\phi(x_i,t_n))+O(\tau+h_{\max}+\eta_k(P)),$$
where $S_{h,\tau}$ is the scheme map, $h_{\max}=\max_jh_j$, $P$ bounds
$|D\phi|$ on the tested compact set, and $\eta_k(P)=0$ for exact control
minimization.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is
$M_K<\infty$ with $|u_\varepsilon(y)|\le M_K$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
and $y\in K$. The **upper half-relaxed limit** and the **lower half-relaxed
limit** of the family, computed in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-epsilon]]), are
$$\overline u(z):=\limsup_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \sup\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\},$$
$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V_k$ be locally bounded periodic interpolant extensions of finite nodal
arrays on grids with $h_k\to0$ and time steps $\tau_k\to0$. Regard this
sequence as the family $V_\epsilon=V_k$ when
$(k+1)^{-1}<\epsilon\le k^{-1}$, and form its upper and lower half-relaxed
limits as in
[[def-half-relaxed-limits]]. If $\overline V-\phi$ has a strict local maximum
at an interior point $z_0=(x_0,t_0)$ for a smooth test $\phi$, then there are
mesh indices $k_m\to\infty$ and grid points $z_m=(x_{i_m},t_{n_m})\to z_0$
such that $V_{k_m}(z_m)-\phi(z_m)\to\overline V(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$ and $z_m$ is
a local maximum of the corresponding nodal values minus $\phi$ on a fixed
closed space-time ball. The lower half-relaxed limit has the dual strict
minimum property. The proof uses Countable Choice only for sequential recovery
from the set-defined half-relaxed limit.

For the continuous first-order Hamiltonian of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]], requiring the subsolution or
supersolution inequality only for smooth ($C^\infty$) local test functions is
equivalent to requiring it for all $C^1$ tests. For the diagonal second-order
operator of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], the
same equivalence holds between smooth tests and all $C^{1,2}$ tests in
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]]. The result is local in
space-time and applies to upper semicontinuous subsolutions and lower
semicontinuous supersolutions.

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. Whenever the controls are
discretized, use a sequence of finite nonempty sets $A_k\subseteq A$ and define
$$H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Define the Hamiltonian error by
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|.$$
The sequence is admissible when $\eta_k(R)\to0$ for every $R<\infty$.
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

Comparison for first-order Hamilton--Jacobi equations, in the two settings of
the design. **(a) The case $O=\mathbb R^n$.** Let $T>0$ and let
$H:\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous for which
there is $C>0$ with
$$|H(x,t,p)-H(y,s,p)|\le C(1+|p|)\,(|x-y|+|t-s|),\qquad |H(x,t,p)-H(x,t,q)|\le C|p-q|$$
for all $x,y,p,q\in\mathbb R^n$ and $t,s\in[0,T]$. Let $u$ be a bounded upper
semicontinuous viscosity subsolution and $v$ a bounded lower semicontinuous
viscosity supersolution of the Cauchy problem in $Z=\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$,
each defined on the closed slab $\mathbb R^n\times[0,T)$ and satisfying the
pointwise initial inequality $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$.
Then $u\le v$ on $Z$. **(b) The compact-cylinder case.** Let
$O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, and let
$H:\overline O\times[0,T]\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and
uniformly continuous in $(x,t)$ uniformly on bounded $p$-sets: there is a
nondecreasing modulus $\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\omega(0+)=0$ such
that
$$|H(x,t,p)-H(y,s,p)|\le\omega\bigl((1+|p|)\,(|x-y|+|t-s|)\bigr)$$
for all $(x,t),(y,s)\in\overline O\times[0,T]$ and all $p\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$u,v$ be continuous on $\overline Z=\overline O\times[0,T]$, $u$ a viscosity
subsolution and $v$ a viscosity supersolution of $u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0$ in $Z$,
with $u\le v$ on the parabolic boundary
$\Gamma=(O\times\{0\})\cup(\partial O\times[0,T])$. Then $u\le v$ on
$\overline Z$. No growth hypothesis on $H$ in the momentum variable is imposed
in this case; the modulus condition replaces it. For an $x$-independent
autonomous Hamiltonian $H(p)$, it holds with the zero modulus. No choice
principle is used.

Let $u_0$ be continuous and periodic, and let $B$ and $L$ bound the drift and
running cost in [[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]]. For the semi-Lagrangian
scheme, if $t_n=n\tau\to0$, $h_{\max}\to0$, and
$h_{\max}^2/\tau\to0$, then
$$\sup_i|U_i^n-u_0(x_i)|\longrightarrow0.$$
For the upwind scheme, the same conclusion holds when $t_n\to0$,
$h_{\max}\to0$, and its CFL condition holds. Both statements are uniform over
all finite control policies and remain true for a finite control discretization.

For the interpolant $I_h$ of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], every cell weight is nonnegative and the weights sum to one by
[[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]. Hence
$V\le W$ on grid nodes implies $I_hV\le I_hW$, and
$\|I_hV\|_{\infty}\le\|V\|_{\infty}$. If $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ and $V_i=\phi(x_i)$, then
$$\|I_hV-\phi\|_{\infty}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2\|\partial_{jj}\phi\|_{\infty}.$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By the stability part of [F1] and $M_k\tau_k=T$, all nodal values satisfy $$\|U_k^n\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty+Lt_n \le\|u_0\|_\infty+LT.$$ The convex interpolation weights give the same bound for $V_k$, so the family is locally bounded on $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$. Form its upper and lower half-relaxed limits $\overline V,\underline V$ as in [F2].

Let $\overline V-\phi$ have a local maximum at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)$, with $\phi$ smooth. Add $\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ to $\phi$; this makes the contact strict without changing its first derivatives at $(x_0,t_0)$, as in [F4]. Choose the nodal local maxima $(x_k,t_k)$ in [F3], with $(x_k,t_k)\to(x_0,t_0)$; write $c_k=U_{i_k}^{n_k}- \phi(x_k,t_k)$. For all sufficiently large $k$, every node used by the previous-time update at $(x_k,t_k)$ lies inside the fixed contact ball: the upwind neighbors are at distance at most $h_{k,\max}$ and each semi-Lagrangian interpolation vertex is at distance at most $\tau_kB+\sqrt d\,h_{k,\max}$. Hence each such previous-layer nodal value satisfies $U_j^{n_k-1}\le\phi(x_j,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k$. Order preservation and constant-shift invariance from [F1] imply $$U_{i_k}^{n_k}=S_k(U^{n_k-1})_{i_k} \le S_k(\phi(\cdot,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k)_{i_k} =S_k(\phi(\cdot,t_k-\tau_k))_{i_k}+c_k.$$ Since $U_{i_k}^{n_k}=\phi(x_k,t_k)+c_k$, the normalized residual is nonpositive. Taking $k\to\infty$ and using the consistency estimate in [F1] gives $\phi_t(x_0,t_0)+H(x_0,t_0,D\phi(x_0,t_0))\le0$. By [F4], $\overline V$ is a viscosity subsolution for the full $C^1$ test class.

At a local minimum of $\underline V-\phi$, subtract $\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ from $\phi$ to make the contact strict without changing its derivatives at $(x_0,t_0)$, as in [F4]. Use the minimizing nodes in [F3]. All previous-layer stencil nodes lie in the contact ball, so $U_j^{n_k-1}\ge\phi(x_j,t_k-\tau_k)+c_k$. Order preservation and constant-shift invariance now yield the reverse update inequality, hence the normalized consistency residual is nonnegative. Passing to the limit gives the viscosity supersolution inequality. The smooth-test equivalence [F4] extends it to every $C^1$ lower test.

The initial trace estimate [F6] and the interpolation error [F7] show that both half-relaxed limits equal $u_0$ on $t=0$. They are bounded by step 1.1 and have the required semicontinuity by [F2]. Apply comparison [F5] to the periodic lifts of $\overline V$ and $\underline V$: it gives $\overline V\le\underline V$. The reverse inequality is part of [F2], so they coincide with a continuous viscosity solution having initial data $u_0$.

Fix $T'<T$ and let $K=[0,1]^d\times[0,T']$ in the periodic lift; it is compact by [F8]. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and write $u$ for the common continuous limit from step 2.3. For $z\in K$ and $q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$, put $P(z,q)$ when the set-defined upper and lower envelopes in [F2] give $$|V_k(y)-u(z)|\le\varepsilon/3\quad\text{for every integer }k\text{ with }1/k<q \text{ and every }y\text{ with }|y-z|<q,$$ and continuity gives $|u(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|y-z|<q$. The family of all balls $$\{B(z,q/2):z\in K,\ q\in\mathbb Q_{>0},\ P(z,q)\}$$ covers $K$: each point has a positive real radius from the two envelope definitions and continuity, and a smaller rational radius still works. This is the family of all qualifying pairs, so no radius is selected for every point. By [F8] take a finite subcover and let $q_*>0$ be its least radius. For $1/k<q_*$, every $y\in K$ lies in one of these balls and therefore $|V_k(y)-u(y)|<2\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$. This proves uniform convergence on the fundamental box through $T'$, hence on the torus and every compact subset of $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$.

risk_review.notes: Checked all six steps against both finite-control schemes and whole-space comparison case (a). Stability is uniform; previous-time upwind nodes and all semi-Lagrangian corners lie within τB+sqrt(d)h of the contact, so both residual signs follow locally. Required τ,h and interpolation/time ratio limits and η_k(P)→0 are present. Initial trace yields both envelopes equal to u0; periodic lifts are bounded USC/LSC and H obeys the exact global space-time/momentum comparison bounds with positive C=max(1,L,B). Comparison identifies envelopes as a continuous viscosity solution. The finite-subcover argument proves convergence of the whole family on compact time slabs including zero, without selecting a point at each mesh. No rate or terminal-T convergence is asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $h_{k,j}\to0$, $\tau_k=T/M_k\to0$, and let $U_k$ be the finite
solutions of [[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]] with its
diffusion-dominance and CFL inequalities at every row. Extend each array
multilinearly in space, constantly on each time interval, and by its initial
interpolant for $-1<t<0$; identify the mesh sequence with the parameter
family convention of [[def-half-relaxed-limits]]. Its upper
half-relaxed limit is a bounded upper semicontinuous viscosity subsolution,
and its lower half-relaxed limit is a bounded lower semicontinuous viscosity
supersolution of the periodic diagonal-diffusion Cauchy problem, with the
respective relaxed initial inequalities equal to $u_0$. This is a stability
statement only; it does not claim that the two limits coincide.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

Let $u$ be upper semicontinuous and $v$ lower semicontinuous on the periodic
space-time cylinder. A **second-order parabolic viscosity subsolution** of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] is a function $u$
such that every $C^{1,2}$ test function $\phi$ for which $u-\phi$ has a local
maximum at $(x_0,t_0)$, $0<t_0<T$, satisfies
$$\phi_t(x_0,t_0)-\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_j\left(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j}\right)(x_0,t_0)+f^a(x_0,t_0)\right\}\le0.$$
Here $C^{1,2}$ means that $\phi_t$, all first spatial derivatives, and all
second spatial derivatives exist and are continuous near the contact point.
A **supersolution** is lower semicontinuous and satisfies the reverse
inequality at every local minimum. A viscosity solution is both. For the Cauchy
problem, the relaxed initial conditions are
$$\limsup_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}u(y,s)\le u_0(x),\qquad \liminf_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}v(y,s)\ge u_0(x).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is

$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.

derivations.claim: Apply [A1] to the upper subsolution and lower supersolution supplied by [F1]. Their common initial trace gives the required ordering, hence $\overline U\le\underline U$. Together with the reverse inequality in [F1], this proves equality.

The common function is both upper and lower semicontinuous by [F1], hence continuous. It is both a viscosity subsolution and supersolution, so is a viscosity solution with the prescribed initial data. Comparison in [A1] implies uniqueness.

Fix $T'<T$ and let $K=[0,1]^d\times[0,T']$ in the periodic lift; this box is compact by Heine--Borel. Write $u$ for the common limit from step 2.1 and fix $\varepsilon>0$. For $z\in K$ and rational $q>0$, include $B(z,q/2)$ in a family when for every integer $k$ with $1/k<q$ and every $y$ with $|y-z|<q$, $|V_k(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$, and continuity gives $|u(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$. The set definitions in [F2] guarantee that these balls cover $K$: each point has a positive real radius, and a smaller rational radius works. The family consists of all qualifying pairs, so no radius is selected point by point. By [F2], a finite subcover exists; take the least of its finitely many rational radii. The triangle inequality then gives $|V_k(y)-u(y)|<2\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$ uniformly on $K$ for all sufficiently large $k$. This proves uniform convergence on the fundamental box through $T'$, hence on the torus and every compact subset of $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$. Thus the extensions converge locally uniformly.

Let $d,q\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty compact subset of
$\mathbb R^q$ (a finite action set is included). For each $a\in A$, let
$b_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,
$$|b_a(x,t)-b_a(y,s)|+|\ell_a(x,t)-\ell_a(y,s)| \le L(|x-y|+|t-s|).$$
Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$
The **periodic first-order controlled Hamilton–Jacobi Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$
The signs are fixed by
$u_t=\min_{a\in A}\{b_a\cdot Du+\ell_a\}$. Whenever the controls are
discretized, use a sequence of finite nonempty sets $A_k\subseteq A$ and define
$$H_k(x,t,p):=\max_{a\in A_k}(-b_a\cdot p-\ell_a).$$
Define the Hamiltonian error by
$$\eta_k(R):=\sup_{x,t,|p|\le R}|H_k(x,t,p)-H(x,t,p)|.$$
The sequence is admissible when $\eta_k(R)\to0$ for every $R<\infty$.
Exact minimization over $A$ corresponds to $\eta_k=0$. Scheme convergence below
uses this explicit control-grid error whenever the controls are discretized.

Use the model and coefficient notation of [[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]] and the periodic grid of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]]. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. Choose a finite nonempty control set $A_k\subseteq A$. For a finite control model take $A_k=A$; for compact controls use a sequence of finite nonempty sets with the stated uniform Hamiltonian error. For each control and grid node put
$$b_{a,j}^+=\max\{b_{a,j},0\},\qquad b_{a,j}^- =\max\{-b_{a,j},0\},$$
and define the explicit row
$$G^a_i(V)=V_i+\tau\left[\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{b_{a,j}^+(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)+\frac{b_{a,j}^-(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i-e_j}-V_i)\right)+\ell_a(x_i,t_n)\right].$$
The periodic HJB upwind update at time $t_n$ is
$$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}G_i^a(U^n).$$
At every step $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, require the CFL condition
$$\tau\max_{a,i}\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{|b_{a,j}(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\le1$$
Initialize $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$. Return $U^M$. Since the transport velocity in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] is $-b_a$ for this Hamiltonian sign convention, the displayed one-sided direction is its sign-reflected upwind row.

derivations.claim: Fix a node $i$. Let $U_j=0$ for every index and let $V_{i-1}=1$ with all other entries zero. Since $N\ge3$, the two neighbors are distinct; hence $U\le V$, while $$S_c(U)_i=0,\qquad \frac{V_{i+1}-V_{i-1}}{2h}=-\frac1{2h},\qquad S_c(V)_i=0+\tau\min\left\{-\frac1{2h},\frac1{2h}\right\} =-\frac{\tau}{2h}<0.$$ Thus $S_c(U)_i>S_c(V)_i$ despite $U\le V$, which disproves monotonicity.

For the same arrays, if $0<\tau/h\le1$, the upwind update at $i$ has the unchanged zero row for action $a=1$ and a nonnegative row value $\tau/h$ for action $a=-1$, so its action minimum is zero. This finite contrast is consistent with the nonnegative CFL weights in [F2].

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ be a nonempty finite state set, let each state $i$
have a nonempty finite ordered action set $A_i$, and let $c>0$. For
$a\in A_i$, choose real coefficients $q^a_{ij}$ satisfying
$$q^a_{ij}\ge0\quad(j\ne i),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}=0,$$
and a reward $r_i^a\in\mathbb R$. The row $q_i^a$ is a conservative generator
row. A deterministic policy is a map $\pi$ with $\pi(i)\in A_i$. Its policy
matrix and reward vector are
$$A^\pi_{ij}=c\,\delta_{ij}-q^{\pi(i)}_{ij},\qquad r^\pi_i=r_i^{\pi(i)}.$$
The **discounted finite-state Bellman system** is
$$cV_i-\max_{a\in A_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^nq^a_{ij}V_j+r_i^a\right)=0, \qquad i\in S.$$
The policy evaluation equation for $\pi$ is $A^\pi V=r^\pi$.

Here $\delta_{ij}$ is $1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

For the finite system of [[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]],
order each finite set $A_i$ by its declared indices and put
$P=\prod_{i\in S}|A_i|$. The procedure takes a positive integer evaluation
budget $K\in\mathbb N$, $K\ge1$ (default $K=P$), and proceeds as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0(i)$ to the least-index action in $A_i$.
2. For the current policy $\pi_k$, solve exactly
   $A^{\pi_k}V^k=r^{\pi_k}$.
3. Form the strict-improvement set
   $$J_k=\left\{i:\max_{a\in A_i}(Q_i^aV^k+r_i^a)>Q_i^{\pi_k(i)}V^k+r_i^{\pi_k(i)}\right\},$$
   where $Q_i^aV=\sum_jq^a_{ij}V_j$.
4. If $J_k=\varnothing$, return $(\texttt{converged},\pi_k,V^k)$.
5. If $J_k\ne\varnothing$ and $k+1=K$, return
   $(\texttt{budget\_exhausted},\pi_k,V^k)$; this status makes no Bellman-solution
   claim.
6. Otherwise, at each $i\in J_k$ switch to the least-index maximizing action
   in $A_i$; retain $\pi_k(i)$ at every state outside $J_k$ and continue.

The policy matrix solve is well-defined by
[[lem-na-discounted-bellman-policy-matrix-inverse-positive]]. A budget of $P$
policy evaluations is sufficient by the theorem below.

For exact policy evaluations, every strict switch in
[[alg-na-finite-control-howard-policy-iteration]] weakly increases the policy
value at every state and strictly increases it at each switched state. No
deterministic policy can recur after a strict switch. With budget
$P=\prod_i|A_i|$, the algorithm terminates within $P$ policy evaluations at
the unique solution of the Bellman system in
[[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]]. A smaller budget may return
`budget_exhausted` without a solution claim.

derivations.claim: Under `(stay, exit)`, the policy equations are $V_1=0$ and $V_2=2$, so $V=(0,2)$. At state $1$, the stay row has value $0$, while the go row has $-V_1+V_2=2>0$; hence the strict-improvement set contains state $1$. At state $2$, both exit actions have value $2=V_2$ and reset has value $V_1-V_2=-2$, so state $2$ is not switched.

The new policy `(go, exit)` solves $2V_1-V_2=0$ and $V_2=2$, hence $V=(1,2)$. At state $1$, go has value $-1+2=1=V_1$ and stay has value $0$; at state $2$, both exit rows remain tied at $2$ and reset has value $1-2=-1$. No strict improvement remains, so the algorithm terminates. The duplicate exit tie is retained exactly as specified, and the strict switch increases state $1$ from $0$ to $1$ as [F2] requires.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

Assume the coefficients are bounded and periodic and a periodic test function
$\phi$ is smooth with bounded derivatives $\phi_{tt}$, $\phi_{x_jx_j}$, and
$\phi_{x_jx_jx_jx_j}$, and the coefficients are bounded. For the scheme of
[[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]], define the normalized
local residual
$$R_{h,\tau}(x_i,t_n)=\frac{\phi(x_i,t_n+\tau)-S_{h,\tau}\phi(\cdot,t_n)_i}{\tau}.$$
Then
$$R_{h,\tau}=\phi_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j})+f^a\right\} +O\left(\tau+\max_j\left[\alpha_{j,\max}h_j^2\|\phi_{x_j^4}\|_\infty+ |b_j|_{\max}h_j\|\phi_{x_jx_j}\|_\infty\right]\right),$$
where $\alpha_{j,\max}:=\sup_{a,x,t}\alpha_j^a(x,t)$ and
$|b_j|_{\max}:=\sup_{a,x,t}|b_j^a(x,t)|$. The bound is uniform over nodes and
times before the terminal step. The $O(\cdot)$ is a
smooth-test residual estimate, not a solution-error rate.

derivations.claim: Direct differentiation gives $u_t=-u$ and $u_{xx}=-4\pi^2u$. Therefore $u_t-u_{xx}=(-1+4\pi^2)u=f$, proving the exact PDE identity in [F1]. The discrete second difference is $$D_{xx}^h u(x_i,t_n)= -\frac{4\sin^2(\pi h)}{h^2}u(x_i,t_n).$$ Taylor expansion in time gives $(u(x_i,t_n+\tau)-u(x_i,t_n))/\tau=u_t(x_i,t_n)+O(\tau)$, while $$u_{xx}-D_{xx}^h u= \left(\frac{4\sin^2(\pi h)}{h^2}-4\pi^2\right)u=O(h^2),$$ because $\sin z=z+O(z^3)$ at $z=0$. Thus the exact normalized residual is $O(\tau+h^2)$, agreeing with [F2]. No accumulated error is claimed.

$\ell_a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and jointly
continuous in $(x,t,a)$. Write $b_a,\ell_a$ also for their periodic lifts to
$\mathbb R^d\times[0,T]$. Assume there are constants $B,L<\infty$ such that
$$|b_a(x,t)|\le B,\qquad |\ell_a(x,t)|\le L,$$
and for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, and $t,s\in[0,T]$,

Given continuous periodic initial data $u_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$H(x,t,p)=\max_{a\in A}\{-b_a(x,t)\cdot p-\ell_a(x,t)\}.$$

$$u_t+H(x,t,Du)=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x).$$

derivations.claim: Away from $x=0,1/2$ and the moving fronts $d_{\mathbb T^1}(x,0)=t$, the function is either constant zero or has $u_t=-1$ and $|u_x|=1$; it satisfies the PDE classically. Near a moving front on the increasing-distance side, put $s=x-t$ in a local lift; on the other side put $s=1-x-t$. In either case $u=\max(s,0)$. There is no $C^1$ upper test at this convex kink: its directional slopes would have to be at least $1$ in the positive $s$ direction and at most $0$ in the negative direction. Any $C^1$ lower test has $s$-slope $p\in[0,1]$. Use a second coordinate tangent to the moving front: the profile is constant in that direction, so the test's tangential derivative is zero. Thus $\phi_t=-p$ and $\phi_x=p$ on the increasing-distance side, or $\phi_x=-p$ on the decreasing-distance side; in both cases its residual is $-p+|p|=0$. At the antipode $x=1/2$ for $t<1/4$, the local profile is $1/2-t-|x-1/2|$. Its upper tests have spatial slope $p\in[-1,1]$ and time derivative $-1$, giving residual $-1+|p|\le0$; no lower test exists at that concave cusp. Thus the sub- and supersolution tests hold everywhere for $0<t<1/4$. The initial trace is $u_0$.

At $x=0$, the sampled data have $U_0=0$ and $U_{\pm1}=h$ because $u_0(\pm h)=h$. For either semi-Lagrangian action the footpoint is $\pm\tau$; linear interpolation between $0$ and $\pm h$ returns $\tau$ when $\tau\le h$, so the action minimum is $\tau$. For the upwind update the forward difference is $1$ and the backward difference is $-1$; multiplying by $a=1$ and $a=-1$, respectively, gives drift contribution $1$ for both actions. The CFL condition is $\tau/h\le1$, so its minimum update is also $\tau$. Since $u(0,\tau)=0$, both one-step errors equal $\tau$. Taking $\tau=h/2$ gives $h^2/\tau=2h\to0$, and [F3] supplies convergence for the refined semi-Lagrangian family under its full hypotheses.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $U$: every $a\in U$ has a neighbourhood on which one finite constant bounds $|f(x)-f(y)|$ by $\|x-y\|_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

derivations.claim: If $U$ is empty, all assertions are vacuous. If $n=0$ and $U$ is nonempty, then $U=\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$, $\partial f(0)=\{0\}$, and $f$ is differentiable with derivative zero. Every localization ball is $\{0\}$; set $H(0)=f(0)$. Then $F^*(0)=-f(0)$ and $g(0)=0$, so the remaining assertions hold directly. Henceforth assume $n\ge1$. At $x\in U$, the directional slope $d(v)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t$ exists and is finite: convexity makes these quotients monotone in $t$, while local Lipschitz continuity bounds them. Positive homogeneity follows by rescaling $t$. Convexity applied at the midpoint of $x+2tv$ and $x+2tw$ gives $d(v+w)\le d(v)+d(w)$. By [A1] and [F2], Hahn-Banach extends zero on $\{0\}$ to a linear functional $p\cdot v\le d(v)$. The chord inequality gives $d(y-x)\le f(y)-f(x)$, so $p\in\partial f(x)$.

If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a ball and $x$ lies in its concentric half ball, testing the support inequality at $x\pm te$ for every unit vector $e$ and sufficiently small $t>0$ gives $|p\cdot e|\le L$. Thus all its subgradients have norm at most $L$. On compact subsets this follows by a finite cover. If $x_j\to x$, $p_j\to p$, and $p_j\in\partial f(x_j)$, pass to the limit in every support inequality using continuity of $f$; hence $p\in\partial f(x)$. Differentiability gives $\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}$ by testing both signs of small increments. Conversely, if $\partial f(x)=\{p\}$, the local bound and [F3] imply that every choice $q_y\in\partial f(y)$ converges to $p$ as $y\to x$: otherwise [A1] selects a contrary sequence with a convergent subsequence whose limit is a different limiting subgradient. The inequalities $p\cdot h\le f(x+h)-f(x)\le q_{x+h}\cdot h$ then prove differentiability with derivative $p$.

Set $H(z)=\sup\{f(x)+p\cdot(z-x):x\in K,\ p\in\partial f(x)\}$. The local bounds from step 2.1 make slopes and intercepts uniformly bounded. Thus this supremum is finite, convex and globally Lipschitz; support inequalities give $H\le f$ on $U$, and the terms at $z=x\in K$ give equality on $K$. This definition uses all supports, without choosing one for each point.

Since $H$ is globally Lipschitz, $F(z)-p\cdot z\to+\infty$ as $|z|\to\infty$. Continuity and compact extreme values give a minimizer. The identity that $F-|\cdot|^2/2$ is convex implies strict convexity of $F$ and uniqueness of this minimizer, denoted $g(p)$. Its minimizing property is exactly $p\in\partial F(g(p))$. More precisely, $p\in\partial F(x)$ iff $p-x\in\partial H(x)$. One direction is immediate. For the other, test the support inequality for $F$ at $x+t(y-x)$, divide by $t>0$, and let $t\downarrow0$; convexity makes the directional slope of $H$ at $x$ no larger than the full chord slope $H(y)-H(x)$, yielding $H(y)-H(x)\ge(p-x)\cdot(y-x)$. Monotonicity of supports of $H$, obtained by adding their two defining inequalities, therefore gives $(p-q)\cdot(g(p)-g(q))\ge |g(p)-g(q)|^2$. Hence $g$ is one-Lipschitz.

The supremum defining $F^*(p)$ is finite and attained uniquely at $g(p)$. Evaluating the two suprema at each other's maximizers gives $0\le F^*(p+k)-F^*(p)-g(p)\cdot k\le (g(p+k)-g(p))\cdot k\le |k|^2$. This proves $DF^*=g$, whose continuity follows from its Lipschitz bound. It also proves the asserted subgradient inverse relation.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $U$: every $a\in U$ has a neighbourhood on which one finite constant bounds $|f(x)-f(y)|$ by $\|x-y\|_2$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.
If $T:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is Lipschitz and $E$ is null, then $T[E]$ is null.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For $u,v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $u_i \le v_i$ for
every $i<n$ write $[u,v]$ for the closed rectangle and
$V(u,v) := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : u_i<x_i<v_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$ for
the open box, both of size $\prod_{i<n}(v_i-u_i)$
([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]); a **closed cube** of side
$\ell \ge 0$ is a set $\prod_{i<n}[c_i,c_i+\ell]$, of size $\ell^{\,n}$. For
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cl}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\operatorname{vol}[u^k,v^k] \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}[u^k,v^k]\Big\},\qquad \lambda^{\mathrm{op}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\prod_{i<n}(v^k_i-u^k_i) \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}V(u^k,v^k)\Big\},$$

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cb}}(E) := \inf\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\ell_k^{\,n} \;:\; E \subseteq \bigcup_{k}\prod_{i<n}[c^k_i,\,c^k_i+\ell_k]\Big\},$$

infima over countable covers of the stated kind, which exist because
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by the rectangles $[-k\mathbf{1},k\mathbf{1}]$, by the
open boxes $V(-k\mathbf{1},k\mathbf{1})$ and by the cubes
$\prod_i[-k,-k+2k]$. Then

$$\lambda^{\mathrm{cl}}(E) \;=\; \lambda^{\mathrm{op}}(E) \;=\; \lambda^{\mathrm{cb}}(E) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(E).$$

Let $n \ge 1$. **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]) is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-outer-measure]]): it vanishes at $\varnothing$, is monotone, and is
countably subadditive.

**The agreement clause is a theorem of ZF and needs no choice principle:**
$\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), where $\mu_0$ is elementary volume. In
particular $\lambda_n^*(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
and $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing) = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

derivations.claim: Shrink to a ball $\overline B_R\subseteq U$ on which $g(x)=f(x)+\lambda|x|^2/2$ is convex and $f(0)>f(x)$ for $0<|x|\le R$. By [F1], $f$ is continuous. Given $0<r<R/4$, the compact annulus $r\le|x|\le R$ has a strictly positive gap $c=f(0)-\max f$. Fix $0<\eta\le\delta$ with $\eta R<c/2$. For every $|q|\le\eta$, all global maximizers of $f(x)+q\cdot x$ on $\overline B_R$ lie in $B_r$, since their value at zero is $f(0)$ and annulus values are at most $f(0)-c+\eta R$. Their maximizing pairs form a closed subset of the compact product $\overline B_R\times\overline B_\eta$, so their set $K$ is compact and lies in $B_r$.

At a maximizing pair $(x,q)$, $f(z)\le f(x)-q\cdot(z-x)$ on $\overline B_R$. Put $v=-q+\lambda x$. Expanding the quadratic gives $g(x+h)\le g(x)+v\cdot h+\lambda|h|^2/2$. Convexity gives the reverse support $g(z)\ge g(x)+v\cdot(z-x)$: for $h=z-x$ and small $t>0$, convexity on the segment from $x-th$ to $z$ yields $g(z)-g(x)\ge(g(x)-g(x-th))/t\ge v\cdot h-\lambda t|h|^2/2$, and let $t\downarrow0$. Thus $f$ is differentiable at $x$, $p_x=Df(x)=-q$, and $f(x)+p_x\cdot(z-x)-\lambda|z-x|^2/2\le f(z)\le f(x)+p_x\cdot(z-x)$ for $z\in\overline B_R$; in particular the slope at each $x\in K$ is unique.

For distinct $x,y\in K$, set $d=y-x$. The support bounds in step 2.1 and $f(y)\le f(x)+p_x\cdot d$ give $(p_x-p_y)\cdot h\le\lambda|d+h|^2/2$ whenever $y+h\in B_R$. If $p_x\ne p_y$, take $h=|d|(p_x-p_y)/|p_x-p_y|$, which is admissible since $|y+h|<3r<R$. Then $|p_x-p_y||d|\le2\lambda|d|^2$. Equal slopes need no estimate, so $x\mapsto p_x$ is $2\lambda$-Lipschitz on $K$.

For each coordinate set $P_j(z)=\inf_{x\in K}(p_x^j+2\lambda|z-x|)$. Compactness makes this finite; the triangle inequality makes it $2\lambda$-Lipschitz, and step 3.1 gives $P_j(x)=p_x^j$ on $K$. Hence $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m)$ is $2\lambda\sqrt m$-Lipschitz and, since each $|q|\le\eta$ has a maximizer in $K$ with $P(x)=-q$, $P(K)\supseteq\overline B_\eta$. If $K$ were null, [F2] would make $P(K)$ null, contradicting the positive outer measure of $B_\eta$; thus $K$ has positive outer measure. If $\lambda=0$, this same construction makes $P$ constant while its image contains $\overline B_\eta$, a contradiction, so no strict-maximum case is missed. Countable Choice required by [F2] follows from [A1].

Since $K$ has positive outer measure, it cannot be contained in the given null set $N$. Choose $x\in K\setminus N$ and its maximizing slope $q$; then $|x|<r$ and $|q|\le\eta\le\delta$. This proves both conclusions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.
Every subset of a null subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is null. Assuming countable choice, every countable union of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ is null.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(P, \le)$ be a
nonempty poset in which **every chain has an upper bound**. Then $P$ has a
maximal element ([[def-maximal-element]]).

Note the hypothesis asks only for an upper bound, not a least upper bound, and
the conclusion asserts only that a maximal element exists, never that a greatest
one does.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply [[thm-recursion]] with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line ([[lem-extended-reals-complete]]). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

derivations.claim: Fix $R\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. For each $p\in C\cap B(0,R)$, differentiability gives a nonempty set of radii $0<r_p<1$ such that $|g(p+h)-g(p)-Dg(p)h|\le\varepsilon|h|$ whenever $|h|\le5r_p$. By [A1], choose one such radius for each $p$. Divide this ball family into dyadic radius classes $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j})$, largest first. In each class use [F3] on the set of subfamilies disjoint from all previously selected balls; the union of any chain is an upper bound, so a maximal disjoint subfamily exists. The union of selected subfamilies is disjoint. It is countable by [F8]: enumerate $\mathbb Q^n$ and assign to each ball the first rational point it contains; disjoint balls get distinct points. If a rejected ball has radius $r$ and meets a selected ball of radius $R_s>r/2$, then $r<2R_s$ and every point of the rejected ball is within $2r+R_s<5R_s$ of the selected center. Thus the fivefold dilates of a countable disjoint subfamily $B(p_i,r_i)$ cover $C\cap B(0,R)$.

Put $v_n=\lambda(B(0,1))$. For any selected ball $B(p_i,r_i)$, the image $g(B(p_i,5r_i))$ lies within distance $5\varepsilon r_i$ of $g(p_i)+Dg(p_i)B(0,5r_i)$. This affine image lies in a disk of radius $5Lr_i$ centered at $g(p_i)$ in an affine subspace of dimension $q\le n-1$. In orthonormal coordinates centered at $g(p_i)$ and adapted to that subspace, the tube lies in a box with $q$ side lengths at most $10Lr_i+10\varepsilon r_i$ and $n-q$ side lengths $10\varepsilon r_i$. Subdivide each side into intervals of length at most $\varepsilon r_i$. The number of resulting boxes is at most $c_n(1+L/\varepsilon)^q$; each is contained in an axis-parallel cube of side at most $c_n\varepsilon r_i$. Since $q\le n-1$ and $\varepsilon<1$, their total cube volume is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$ for a finite constant $C_n\ge1$ depending only on $n$. This constructs actual null covers without a rotation-invariance theorem or an area formula.

The selected balls lie in $B(0,R+1)$ and are pairwise disjoint. By [F5], each has measure $v_n r_i^n$, and the containing ball has measure $v_n(R+1)^n$. Countable additivity and monotonicity [F6] give $\sum_i r_i^n\le(R+1)^n$, using $v_n>0$. The Countable Choice hypotheses of [F5] and [F6] follow from [A1].

The fivefold balls in step 1.1 cover $C\cap B(0,R)$, and step 1.2 supplies a finite cube cover of each corresponding image with total volume at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$. By [A1], choose one such finite cover for each selected ball. Index these cubes by $(i,j)$; [F7] enumerates the resulting subset of $\mathbb N^2$. Every finite partial sum is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}\sum_i r_i^n\le C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n$ by [F9] and step 2.1. For any cover budget $\delta>0$, take $\varepsilon=\min\{1/2,\delta/[C_n(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n]\}>0$; the bound is then at most $\delta$. By [F1], $g(C\cap B(0,R))$ is null.

The set $C$ is the union of $C\cap B(0,R)$ over integers $R\ge1$. Each image in this countable union is null by step 3.1; [F2] therefore gives that $g(C)$ is null. Its Countable Choice hypothesis follows from [A1].
