citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
Let $u\in L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ have one measurable ACL
representative $u^*$, and suppose measurable functions
$g_i\in L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, $1\le i\le n$, satisfy the
following: on almost every line parallel to the $i$th coordinate axis, the
one-dimensional derivative of the ACL section of $u^*$ exists and equals the
section of $g_i$ almost everywhere. Then $g_i$ is the weak derivative
$D_i u$ for every $i$, that is,
$$\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi\,dx\qquad(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)).$$
The integrals are bilinear, without conjugation. If $\Omega=\varnothing$,
the assertion is vacuous.

The Axiom of Choice is used only to invoke the cited Countable Choice and
Dependent Choice interfaces for completed-product Fubini and one-dimensional
absolute-continuity integration by parts; no representative is selected in
the proof.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, $B=B(x_0,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $r>0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and $u\in W^{1,p}(B;\mathbb K)$ with ball average $u_B=|B|^{-1}\int_Bu$. Then $\|u-u_B\|_{L^p(B)}\le C(n,p)\,r\,\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}$.
Every subset of a null subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is null. Assuming countable choice, every countable union of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ is null.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $m \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$,

$$\lambda_m^*(E) = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E \text{ is null},$$

nullity being the covering notion of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]:
that is, if and only if for every real $\varepsilon>0$ the set $E$ is covered by
a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at
most $\varepsilon$.

derivations.claim: Fix a scalar component and a ball compactly contained in a neighborhood where it is $L$-Lipschitz. Each coordinate section is Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous by [F2], and has a derivative almost everywhere by [F3], bounded by $L$. For measurability, write the limsup and liminf of the coordinate difference quotients as countable suprema and infima over rational increments; continuity of the section makes these equal the corresponding real-increment limits. Define $g_i$ by their common finite limit where it exists and by zero elsewhere. Fubini makes the measurable exceptional set have Lebesgue measure zero; [F11] converts it to closed-cube-cover nullity. The continuous function is an ACL representative, so [F1] gives $D_i u=g_i$ weakly and $u\in W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

Outside a null set, $x$ is a strong Lebesgue point of $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n)$. For each rational vector $q\in\mathbb Q^n$, apply [F4] locally to the scalar functions $|g-q|$ and to the components of $g$. On a fixed bounded Lipschitz ball these functions are integrable; extend them by zero to $\mathbb R^n$ to apply [F4], and restrict to interior points, where sufficiently small ball averages are unchanged. For each application, the almost-everywhere conclusion provides a measurable Lebesgue-measure-zero set containing the exceptions. Convert that set to closed-cube-cover nullity by [F11], then remove the countable union of these cube-cover-null sets using [F6]. At each remaining point, for every rational $q$, $$\limsup_{r\downarrow0}\frac{1}{\lambda(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\,dy\le 2|q-g(x)|.$$ Rational vectors approximate $g(x)$ by [F10], so this limit is zero. The rational balls whose closures lie in neighborhoods on which the chosen component is Lipschitz form a countable cover of $U$: local Lipschitz continuity gives a suitable ball around each point, density of rational centers/radii gives a rational subball, and [A1] selects one Lipschitz neighborhood and constant for each such ball. Apply the local argument on these balls.

Fix such a point $x$, put $p=g(x)$, and on $B(x,r)\Subset U$ set $w(y)=u(y)-u(x)-p\cdot(y-x)$. The function $w$ is bounded on this ball. By [F1] and linearity of the test-function identity, its weak gradient is $g(y)-p$, which is bounded there; thus $w\in W^{1,1}(B(x,r))$ by [F9]. Also $w(x)=0$ and $w$ is $(L+|p|)$-Lipschitz. The strong Lebesgue-point property and [F8] give $\int_{B(x,r)}|Dw|=o(r^n)$. Applying [F5] yields $$\int_{B(x,r)}|w-w_{B(x,r)}|=o(r^{n+1}).$$

Write $M=L+|p|$. If $M=0$, $w$ vanishes on every sufficiently small ball. Otherwise fix $\epsilon>0$. If $|w_{B(x,r)}|\ge\epsilon r$, then on $B(x,c r)$, with $c=\min\{1/2,\epsilon/(2M)\}$, the Lipschitz bound and $w(x)=0$ give $|w-w_{B(x,r)}|\ge\epsilon r/2$. Since $\lambda(B(x,c r))=v_n c^n r^n$ by [F8], the integral in step 3.1 would be at least $v_n c^n\epsilon r^{n+1}/2$, a contradiction for all sufficiently small $r$. Hence $w_{B(x,r)}=o(r)$. If some $y\in B(x,r/2)$ had $|w(y)|\ge\epsilon r$, then for small $r$ we would have $|w(y)-w_{B(x,r)}|\ge\epsilon r/2$. On $B(y,c' r)\subset B(x,r)$, where $c'=\min\{1/4,\epsilon/(4M)\}$, Lipschitz continuity gives $|w-w_{B(x,r)}|\ge\epsilon r/4$. Its integral is at least $v_n(c')^n\epsilon r^{n+1}/4$, again contradicting step 3.1. Thus $\sup_{B(x,r/2)}|w|=o(r)$. For $h\ne0$, take $r=3|h|$, so $x+h\in B(x,r/2)$; this yields the Frechet expansion $u(x+h)-u(x)-p\cdot h=o(|h|)$.

The countable rational-ball basis [F10] and the finitely many real components of $u$ produce one exceptional cube-cover-null set by [F6] and the definition [F7]. The component derivatives assemble into the Frechet derivative. The full Axiom of Choice is used through the stated ACL, Fubini, differentiation, null-union and Poincare suppliers; no reduction to Countable Choice is asserted.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Then $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $U$: every $a\in U$ has a neighbourhood on which one finite constant bounds $|f(x)-f(y)|$ by $\|x-y\|_2$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $u:U\to\mathbb R$, and $z\in U$. Write $\mathbb S^m$ for the real symmetric $m$ by $m$ matrices. The second-order elliptic superjet consists of pairs $(p,X)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb S^m$ such that
$$u(z+h)\le u(z)+p\cdot h+\tfrac12 h^{\mathsf T}Xh+o(|h|^2)\quad(h\to0).$$
Here the inequality means that its positive remainder divided by $|h|^2$ has limit zero. Denote this set by $J^{2,+}u(z)$. Define
$$J^{2,-}u(z)=-J^{2,+}(-u)(z).$$
The closed superjet $\overline J^{2,+}u(z)$ consists of all limits $(p,X)$ for which there are $z_n\in U$ and $(p_n,X_n)\in J^{2,+}u(z_n)$ satisfying
$$(z_n,u(z_n),p_n,X_n)\longrightarrow(z,u(z),p,X).$$
Define $\overline J^{2,-}u(z)=-\overline J^{2,+}(-u)(z)$. The value convergence is part of the definition. The same definitions work for functions allowed to equal $-\infty$ away from the finite base point, with all approximating base values finite. A two-sided quadratic expansion means that both the upper and lower inequalities hold with the same $(p,X)$; it is also called a second-order Peano expansion. Matrix order means $X\le Y$ iff $h^{\mathsf T}Xh\le h^{\mathsf T}Yh$ for every $h$.

For space-time $z=(t,x)$ this is the full Euclidean jet, whose matrix also has time and mixed entries. No assertion about parabolic jets is included in this definition.

derivations.claim: The maximum exists by [F1], is finite above by $\max_K v$, and is finite below by evaluating at any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Expanding the square gives $\widehat v(\xi)+\lambda|\xi|^2/2=\sup_{x\in K}\{v(x)-\lambda|x|^2/2+\lambda x\cdot\xi\}$. Every expression in the supremum is affine in $\xi$, so the supremum is convex; finiteness and [F2] give continuity and the asserted semiconvexity.

Fix a maximizer $y$ at $\eta$. Evaluation at $y$ and the upper-jet inequality [F3] give, for small $h$, $\lambda(y-\eta)\cdot h-\lambda|h|^2/2\le\widehat v(\eta+h)-\widehat v(\eta)\le q\cdot h+h^{\mathsf T}Yh/2+o(|h|^2)$. Put $h=te$ for every unit $e$ and both signs of $t$, divide by $|t|$, and let $t\to0$; then $\lambda(y-\eta)=q$, so the maximizer is unique and the value identity follows. For $x$ near $y$, set $\xi=\eta+x-y$, so the penalty is unchanged; the same jet inequality gives $v(x)-v(y)\le\widehat v(\eta+x-y)-\widehat v(\eta)\le q\cdot(x-y)+(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Y(x-y)/2+o(|x-y|^2)$. This is the transferred upper jet, and for an interior $y$ the extension and original function agree locally.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and locally Lipschitz map $u:U\to\mathbb R^m$ (each point has a neighborhood on which $|u(y)-u(z)|\le L|y-z|$ for some finite $L$, [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), $u$ is Frechet differentiable outside a null subset of $U$. Here Frechet differentiability at $x$ means that a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ satisfies $u(x+h)=u(x)+Ah+o(|h|)$.
If $T:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is Lipschitz and $E$ is null, then $T[E]$ is null.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), where $n\ge1$. Write $B(x,r)$ for the Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]). Let
$$C=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(p+h)=g(p)+Dg(p)h+o(|h|)\text{ as }h\to0,\ \det Dg(p)=0\}.$$
Then $g(C)$ is null in $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f$ be finite convex, in the sense of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]], on an open convex $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. At each $x\in U$ the subdifferential $\partial f(x)=\{p:f(y)\ge f(x)+p\cdot(y-x)\ (y\in U)\}$ is nonempty; it is locally bounded and its graph is locally closed. It is a singleton exactly when $f$ is differentiable, and then equals $\{Df(x)\}$. For every closed Euclidean ball $K\subset U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is a finite globally Lipschitz convex $H$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]) on $\mathbb R^n$ equal to $f$ on $K$. For $F(x)=H(x)+|x|^2/2$, the conjugate $F^*(p)=\sup_x(p\cdot x-F(x))$ is finite and $C^1$, and $g=DF^*$ is globally one-Lipschitz with $g(p)=x$ iff $p\in\partial F(x)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
Every subset of a null subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is null. Assuming countable choice, every countable union of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ is null.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

derivations.claim: First consider a finite convex function $f$ on an open ball. Localize on a smaller closed ball $K$ and use [F4] to obtain a finite globally Lipschitz convex $H=f$ on $K$, then set $F=H+|\cdot|^2/2$ and $g=DF^*$, which is globally one-Lipschitz and satisfies $g(q)=x$ exactly when $q\in\partial F(x)$. By [F1], the nondifferentiability set $N$ of $g$ is null; [F2] makes $g(N)$ null, and [F3] makes $g(C)$ null for the differentiable singular-derivative set $C$ of $g$. The locally Lipschitz function $F$ is differentiable outside another null set $M$ by [F1]. The union $M\cup g(N)\cup g(C)$ is null by [F6]. For $x$ in the interior of $K$ outside that union, set $p=DF(x)$. Then $g(p)=x$, $g$ is differentiable at $p$, and $B=Dg(p)$ is invertible. Full AC is used by the stated suppliers and to choose the localizations simultaneously.

As $y\to x$, every $q\in\partial F(y)$ tends to $p$, uniformly over all such subgradients: otherwise, by [A1], choose $y_k\to x$ and $q_k\in\partial F(y_k)$ staying a fixed distance from $p$; local boundedness in [F4] and [F5] give a convergent subsequence, and the locally closed graph in [F4] puts its limit in $\partial F(x)=\{p\}$, a contradiction. Since $g(q)=y$, differentiability of $g$ at $p$ gives $y-x=B(q-p)+o(|q-p|)$. Invertibility absorbs the remainder to give $|q-p|\le2\|B^{-1}\||y-x|$ for nearby $y$, hence $q=p+B^{-1}(y-x)+o(|y-x|)$ uniformly for every $q\in\partial F(y)$.

Fix a small $h$. The section $t\mapsto F(x+th)$ is Lipschitz on $[0,1]$, hence absolutely continuous by [F7]. Wherever its derivative exists, the two support inequalities in directions $h$ and $-h$ show that it equals $q\cdot h$ for every $q\in\partial F(x+th)$. By step 2.1, for every $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently small $|h|$, $$|q-p-B^{-1}(th)|\le\epsilon t|h|$$ for every $0<t\le1$ and every such $q$. Integrating the measurable scalar derivative using [F7] gives $$|F(x+h)-F(x)-p\cdot h-\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}h|\le\epsilon|h|^2/2.$$ No measurable subgradient selection is used. Replace $B^{-1}$ by its symmetric part, which has the same quadratic form.

Subtract $|x|^2/2$ to obtain the quadratic expansion for $f$ in the interior of $K$. Exhaust the original ball by countably many smaller closed balls and discard their null exceptional sets using [F6, F8]. The family of rational balls whose closures lie inside a local semiconvexity ball is countable and covers $U$; by [A1] choose a corresponding finite convexity constant for each. Apply the convex conclusion to $u+c|\cdot|^2/2$ on each ball and subtract that quadratic. Countable unions remain null by [F6, F8], and the remainder is direction-uniform by step 3.1. Full AC is retained; no reduction to Countable Choice is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $u:U\to\mathbb R$, and $z\in U$. Write $\mathbb S^m$ for the real symmetric $m$ by $m$ matrices. The second-order elliptic superjet consists of pairs $(p,X)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb S^m$ such that
$$u(z+h)\le u(z)+p\cdot h+\tfrac12 h^{\mathsf T}Xh+o(|h|^2)\quad(h\to0).$$
Here the inequality means that its positive remainder divided by $|h|^2$ has limit zero. Denote this set by $J^{2,+}u(z)$. Define
$$J^{2,-}u(z)=-J^{2,+}(-u)(z).$$
The closed superjet $\overline J^{2,+}u(z)$ consists of all limits $(p,X)$ for which there are $z_n\in U$ and $(p_n,X_n)\in J^{2,+}u(z_n)$ satisfying
$$(z_n,u(z_n),p_n,X_n)\longrightarrow(z,u(z),p,X).$$
Define $\overline J^{2,-}u(z)=-\overline J^{2,+}(-u)(z)$. The value convergence is part of the definition. The same definitions work for functions allowed to equal $-\infty$ away from the finite base point, with all approximating base values finite. A two-sided quadratic expansion means that both the upper and lower inequalities hold with the same $(p,X)$; it is also called a second-order Peano expansion. Matrix order means $X\le Y$ iff $h^{\mathsf T}Xh\le h^{\mathsf T}Yh$ for every $h$.

For space-time $z=(t,x)$ this is the full Euclidean jet, whose matrix also has time and mixed entries. No assertion about parabolic jets is included in this definition.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty compact, let $v:K\to\mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous (so $\limsup_{y\to x}v(y)\le v(x)$ for each $x\in K$), and extend $v$ by $-\infty$ off $K$. For $\lambda>0$ define
$$\widehat v(\xi)=\max_{x\in K}\{v(x)-\tfrac\lambda2|x-\xi|^2\}.$$
This is finite, continuous and $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R^m$, meaning that $\widehat v(\xi)+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ is convex ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]). If $(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}\widehat v(\eta)$, every maximizing point equals $y=\eta+q/\lambda$, and
$$(q,Y)\in J^{2,+}v(y),\qquad v(y)=\widehat v(\eta)+\frac{|q|^2}{2\lambda}.$$
The jets of $v$ are understood for its extended function, or for its original local domain if $y$ is interior to $K$. These conclusions use no choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $u:U\to\mathbb R$ be locally semiconvex: around each point there is a Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]) and $c\ge0$ such that $x\mapsto u(x)+c|x|^2/2$ is convex in the sense of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]. Outside a set null in the cube-cover sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]], there are $p\in\mathbb R^n$ and a symmetric matrix $A$ with
$$u(x+h)=u(x)+p\cdot h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}Ah+o(|h|^2)\quad(h\to0).$$
The remainder is uniform in direction. In particular $u$ is twice differentiable in the Peano sense almost everywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f$ be finite and locally semiconvex near $0\in\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$: on some Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]), $f(x)+\lambda|x|^2/2$ is convex ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]) for a finite $\lambda\ge0$. Suppose $0$ is a strict local maximum of $f$. For every sufficiently small $r>0$ and every $\delta>0$, the set of points $x\in B_r(0)$ where $f(x)+q\cdot x$ has a local maximum for some $|q|\le\delta$ contains a compact subset of positive Lebesgue outer measure. Consequently, given any Lebesgue null set $N$, such a maximum can be chosen with $x\notin N$, $|x|<r$, and $|q|\le\delta$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

derivations.claim: First prove the quadratic compactly localized case. Translate to $z=0$, subtract $u_i(0)$ and the affine terms $D_i\phi(0)\cdot x_i$, and suppose $u_i(0)=0$ and $w(x):=\sum_i u_i(x_i)\le x^{\mathsf T}Ax/2$ on compact neighborhoods $K_i$ of zero. Extend the restrictions by $-\infty$ off $K_i$, set $\lambda=\varepsilon^{-1}+\|A\|>0$ and $B=A+\varepsilon A^2$, and write $h=x-\xi$. The identity $|\varepsilon^{-1/2}h-\varepsilon^{1/2}A\xi|^2\ge0$ gives $x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi+\lambda|x-\xi|^2$. Define $\widehat u_i$ by [F2] and $f(\xi)=\sum_i\widehat u_i(\xi_i)$. The supremum separates over the finite compact product, so $f(\xi)=\sup_x\{w(x)-\lambda|x-\xi|^2/2\}\le\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi/2$. Each $\widehat u_i(0)\ge0$, while $f(0)\le0$, so all are zero; also $f+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ is convex.

The function $F(\xi)=f(\xi)-\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi/2-|\xi|^4$ has a strict maximum at zero and is locally semiconvex, since the Hessian of the subtracted polynomial is bounded on every fixed ball. Apply [F3] outside the null set where $f$ lacks a Peano expansion: for each $n$, [A1] selects $|\xi_n|<1/n$, $|q_n|\le1/n$ so $F+q_n\cdot\xi$ has a local maximum at $\xi_n$ and $f$ has expansion $(p_n,Z_n)$ there. Restricting to lines gives $p_n=B\xi_n+4|\xi_n|^2\xi_n-q_n$ and $Z_n\le B+8\xi_n\xi_n^{\mathsf T}+4|\xi_n|^2I$; convexity of $f+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ gives $Z_n\ge-\lambda I$. Thus $p_n\to0$ and $Z_n$ is bounded. AC supplies the countable selections and is inherited from [F3].

Separability makes $Z_n$ block diagonal: each coordinate restriction gives the corresponding Peano expansion of $\widehat u_i$, and summing those expansions gives a second expansion of $f$ with Hessian $\operatorname{diag}(Z_{n,11},\ldots,Z_{n,kk})$. Uniqueness follows because a quadratic form that is $o(|h|^2)$ vanishes on every direction and hence by polarization. Set $X_{n,i}=Z_{n,ii}$. The transfer in [F2] gives $y_{n,i}=\xi_{n,i}+p_{n,i}/\lambda$, $(p_{n,i},X_{n,i})\in J^{2,+}u_i(y_{n,i})$, and $u_i(y_{n,i})=\widehat u_i(\xi_{n,i})+|p_{n,i}|^2/(2\lambda)$. Since $y_{n,i}\to0$, they eventually lie inside $K_i$; continuity of $\widehat u_i$ gives $u_i(y_{n,i})\to0=u_i(0)$.

By [F4], extract one subsequence along which the finitely many entries of $Z_n$ converge to $Z=\operatorname{diag}(X_i)$. The inequalities in step 2.1 pass to the limit, giving $-\lambda I\le Z\le B$. The convergent jets and values from step 3.1 imply $(0,X_i)\in\overline J^{2,+}u_i(0)$ by [F1]; this proves the localized quadratic case.

For the general case, translate and subtract affine functions as above. Taylor's formula gives $\phi(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax/2+o(|x|^2)$, so for every sufficiently small $\eta>0$ there are compact neighborhoods $K_i^\eta$ with $\sum_i u_i(x_i)\le x^{\mathsf T}(A+\eta I)x/2$. Apply the quadratic case from step 4.1 with $A_\eta=A+\eta I$; it gives closed jets $(0,X_i^\eta)$ with $-(\varepsilon^{-1}+\|A_\eta\|)I\le\operatorname{diag}(X_i^\eta)\le A_\eta+\varepsilon A_\eta^2$. Because zero is interior to each $K_i^\eta$, localization does not change these closed jets.

Take $\eta_n=1/n$ and, by [A1], choose for each sufficiently large $n$ one tuple of closed-jet matrices supplied by step 5.1. Use [F4] to extract a convergent subsequence of these block matrices. The limit obeys the required bounds because $\|A+\eta I\|\to\|A\|$. For each closed jet $(0,X_i^\eta)$, [A1] selects an actual approximating jet with point, value, gradient, and matrix within $1/n$; the defining value-sensitive closure [F1] then gives the limiting closed jet. Restoring the subtracted affine terms gives gradient $D_i\phi(z)$, and negating jets proves the lower-semicontinuous version.

Let $u$ be upper semicontinuous and $v$ lower semicontinuous on the periodic
space-time cylinder. A **second-order parabolic viscosity subsolution** of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] is a function $u$
such that every $C^{1,2}$ test function $\phi$ for which $u-\phi$ has a local
maximum at $(x_0,t_0)$, $0<t_0<T$, satisfies
$$\phi_t(x_0,t_0)-\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_j\left(\alpha_j^a\phi_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a\phi_{x_j}\right)(x_0,t_0)+f^a(x_0,t_0)\right\}\le0.$$
Here $C^{1,2}$ means that $\phi_t$, all first spatial derivatives, and all
second spatial derivatives exist and are continuous near the contact point.
A **supersolution** is lower semicontinuous and satisfies the reverse
inequality at every local minimum. A viscosity solution is both. For the Cauchy
problem, the relaxed initial conditions are
$$\limsup_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}u(y,s)\le u_0(x),\qquad \liminf_{(y,s)\to(x,0),\ s>0}v(y,s)\ge u_0(x).$$

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

and
$$-\left(\varepsilon^{-1}+\|A\|\right)I\ \le\ \operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\ \le\ A+\varepsilon A^2.$$
Here all jets are full Euclidean jets. In particular one may take each $U_i$ to be a space-time domain of dimension $d+1$. For a lower semicontinuous function $v$, applying the theorem to $-v$ and then negating its jet gives the corresponding closed subjet for $v$.

Let $u$ be a USC viscosity subsolution in the sense of
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]], and write the local
space-time variable as $z=(t,x)$. If
$((a,p),H)\in\overline J^{2,+}u(t,x)$ is a closed elliptic jet in all $d+1$
variables ([[def-na-second-order-elliptic-semijets-and-closure]]), and $X$ is the spatial
principal block of $H$, then
$$a-\max_{c\in A}\left\{\sum_j(\alpha_j^c(x,t)X_{jj}+b_j^c(x,t)p_j)+f^c(x,t)\right\}\le0.$$
For an LSC supersolution and a closed elliptic subjet the reverse inequality
holds. All points are interior in time; local periodic lifts are understood.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For any fixed lifts, a lattice minimizer exists: only finitely many integer vectors can give a norm no larger than the norm at $k=0$. If a minimizing difference $r$ has $|r|=D(x,y)<1/2$, then for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, $|k|\ge1$ and $r\cdot k\ge-|r||k|$: for $r\ne0$ this follows by expanding $\bigl||k|r+|r|k\bigr|^2\ge0$, and for $r=0$ it is immediate. Consequently $$|r+k|^2-|r|^2=|k|^2+2r\cdot k\ge |k|(|k|-2|r|)>0.$$ Thus that minimizing difference is unique. Choose continuous local lifts near $x,y$ and keep the minimizing lattice vector fixed; their resulting difference $r^{\prime}$ stays of norm less than $1/2$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood. The same inequality for every nonzero $k$ shows that this difference remains the unique minimizer throughout that neighborhood. Hence there $D^2=|r^{\prime}|^2$, a smooth quadratic in the local coordinates, justifying [F5].

Define $u(x,0)$ as the raw upper trace and $v(x,0)$ as the raw lower trace. Boundedness makes them finite. For example, if $x_k\to x$ and $u(x_k,0)$ approaches its limsup, the raw upper-trace definition and [A1] let us select interior $(y_k,t_k)$ with $|y_k-x_k|+t_k<1/k$ and $u(y_k,t_k)>u(x_k,0)-1/k$. Thus $y_k\to x$, $t_k\to0$, and $\limsup_k u(x_k,0)\le u(x,0)$. The lower-trace argument is dual. For a sequence with positive times tending to zero, the raw trace definition gives the USC/LSC inequalities directly; splitting a mixed sequence into positive-time and initial-edge subsequences proves the extensions are USC/LSC on the closed initial edge. The assumed order gives $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$. Assume for contradiction that $u(x_*,t_*)-v(x_*,t_*)>0$ at some $0<t_*<T$. Choose $S$ with $t_*<S<T$, then choose $\eta,\gamma>0$ sufficiently small that $$m:=u(x_*,t_*)-v(x_*,t_*)-\eta t_*-\gamma/(S-t_*)>0.$$ Put $P(t)=\eta t+\gamma/(S-t)$. If $u(x,t)-v(y,s)-P(t)\ge0$, boundedness bounds $P(t)$ above by $\|u\|_\infty+\|v\|_\infty$, so $t\le S-c$ for some $c>0$.

Using [F5], define $$M_\varepsilon=\max_{x,y\in\mathbb T^d,\ 0\le t<S}\{u(x,t)-v(y,t)-P(t)-D(x,y)^2/(2\varepsilon)\}.$$ The maximum exists by step 1.2 and [F4]: the expression is USC, and its positive superlevel sets stay in a compact time interval bounded away from $S$. Also $M_\varepsilon\ge m$. Write $M_0=\max_{x,\ 0\le t<S}(u(x,t)-v(x,t)-P(t))\ge m$, also attained. At any maximizing triple $(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon,t_\varepsilon)$, boundedness gives $D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon)^2=O(\varepsilon)$. Compactness and semicontinuity imply $M_\varepsilon\to M_0$: for every sequence $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, a subsequence of maximizers tends to $(x,x,t)$, and the limsup of the unpenalized expression is at most $M_0$, whereas $M_\varepsilon\ge M_0$. Moreover $$0\le D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon)^2/(4\varepsilon)\le M_{2\varepsilon}-M_\varepsilon\longrightarrow0,$$ by evaluating the $2\varepsilon$ maximum at an $\varepsilon$ maximizer. These conclusions hold uniformly over maximizing triples, by the same sequential compactness argument. No sequence of these maximizers can have $t_\varepsilon\to0$: then $x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon\to x$ along a subsequence and semicontinuity and the initial order give limsup of their maximum values at most $-P(0)<0$, contradicting $M_\varepsilon\ge m$.

For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, introduce independent times and maximize $$\Phi_{\varepsilon,\delta}(x,t,y,s)=u(x,t)-v(y,s)-P(t)-D(x,y)^2/(2\varepsilon)-(t-s)^2/(2\delta)$$ over $x,y\in\mathbb T^d$, $0\le t<S$, $0\le s\le S$. Maxima exist by step 1.2 and [F4] and are at least $M_\varepsilon\ge m$. Boundedness gives $|t-s|=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $t\le S-c$ uniformly. For fixed $\varepsilon$, compactness shows that as $\delta\downarrow0$ every limit of maximizing quadruples is a synchronized maximizer of $M_\varepsilon$: the limsup of the expression without the temporal penalty is at most $M_\varepsilon$, while the maximum is at least $M_\varepsilon$. Hence the temporal penalty tends to zero too. By step 2.1 and [F5], for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ these limiting times are positive and the spatial distance is less than $1/2$. Consequently for each such $\varepsilon$ and all sufficiently small $\delta$, both times are strictly in $(0,S)$ and $D(x,y)^2=|r|^2$ is smooth near the maximizer in local lifts with $r=x-y$ and $|r|=D(x,y)$. Thus all contacts used next are interior in the original cylinder.

At such a maximizer apply [F2] to $u(t,x)$ and $-v(s,y)$ with $$\phi(t,x,s,y)=|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)+(t-s)^2/(2\delta)+P(t),\qquad\mu=\varepsilon.$$ It gives a closed upper jet of $u$ with gradient $(a,p)$ and Hessian $H$, and a closed lower jet of $v$ with gradient $(b,p)$ and Hessian $K$, where $$p=r/\varepsilon,\quad a=(t-s)/\delta+P'(t),\quad b=(t-s)/\delta,\quad a-b=P'(t)\ge\eta.$$ Negating the jet of $-v$ gives the lower jet of $v$ directly from its defining expansion and witnessing sequence. Let $X,Y$ be the spatial principal blocks of $H,K$. The full Hessian of $\phi$ has no space-time mixed entries. Its spatial block is $\varepsilon^{-1}B$ with $B=\begin{pmatrix}I&-I\\-I&I\end{pmatrix}$ and $B^2=2B$. Restricting the upper matrix inequality in [F2] to vectors with zero temporal components therefore gives $$\begin{pmatrix}X&0\\0&-Y\end{pmatrix}\le(3/\varepsilon)B.$$ The temporal Hessian, including $P''(t)$ and the potentially large $1/\delta$, contributes nothing to this spatial restriction.

For each control $c$ write $G_c(x,t,p,X)=\sum_j(\alpha_j^c(x,t)X_{jj}+b_j^c(x,t)p_j)+f^c(x,t)$. By [F3], $a\le\max_cG_c(x,t,p,X)$ and $b\ge\max_cG_c(y,s,p,Y)$. Finiteness gives $$\eta\le a-b\le\max_c\{G_c(x,t,p,X)-G_c(y,s,p,Y)\}.$$ For $\sigma_j^c=\sqrt{\alpha_j^c}$, rationalization and [F1] give $$|\sigma_j^c(x,t)-\sigma_j^c(y,s)|\le\frac{L}{2\sqrt{\alpha_*}}(|r|+|t-s|).$$ Evaluate the spatial matrix inequality of step 4.1 on each vector $(\sigma_j^c(x,t)e_j,\sigma_j^c(y,s)e_j)$ and sum over $j$ to obtain $$\sum_j(\alpha_j^c(x,t)X_{jj}-\alpha_j^c(y,s)Y_{jj})\le\frac3\varepsilon\sum_j|\sigma_j^c(x,t)-\sigma_j^c(y,s)|^2\le\frac{3dL^2}{4\alpha_*\varepsilon}(|r|+|t-s|)^2.$$ The drift difference is bounded by $C(|r|+|t-s|)|r|/\varepsilon$, and the forcing difference by $L(|r|+|t-s|)$, uniformly over the finite controls, using [F1]. Hence a constant $C$ independent of $\varepsilon,\delta$ satisfies $$\eta\le C\left\{\frac{(|r|+|t-s|)^2}{\varepsilon}+\frac{(|r|+|t-s|)|r|}{\varepsilon}+|r|+|t-s|\right\}.$$

First let $\delta\downarrow0$ for fixed $\varepsilon$, selecting a convergent subsequence of maximizing quadruples by [A1] and [F4]. Since $\varepsilon$ is fixed, every term containing $|t-s|/\varepsilon$ vanishes. The remaining spatial pair is a maximizer of $M_\varepsilon$, so step 5.1 gives $\eta\le C'(D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon)^2/\varepsilon+D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon))$. Now let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Both terms vanish by step 2.1, contradicting $\eta>0$. The assumed positive gap is impossible, so $u\le v$ at every interior point. The initial-edge assertion is its assumed order.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $h_{k,j}\to0$, $\tau_k=T/M_k\to0$, and let $U_k$ be the finite
solutions of [[alg-na-explicit-diagonal-diffusion-hjb-grid-step]] with its
diffusion-dominance and CFL inequalities at every row. Extend each array
multilinearly in space, constantly on each time interval, and by its initial
interpolant for $-1<t<0$; identify the mesh sequence with the parameter
family convention of [[def-half-relaxed-limits]]. Its upper
half-relaxed limit is a bounded upper semicontinuous viscosity subsolution,
and its lower half-relaxed limit is a bounded lower semicontinuous viscosity
supersolution of the periodic diagonal-diffusion Cauchy problem, with the
respective relaxed initial inequalities equal to $u_0$. This is a stability
statement only; it does not claim that the two limits coincide.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let
$(u_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}$ be a family of real-valued functions on
$U$ that is **locally bounded**: for every compact $K\subseteq U$ there is
$M_K<\infty$ with $|u_\varepsilon(y)|\le M_K$ for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
and $y\in K$. The **upper half-relaxed limit** and the **lower half-relaxed
limit** of the family, computed in $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-epsilon]]), are
$$\overline u(z):=\limsup_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\inf_{\delta>0}\ \sup\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\},$$
$$\underline u(z):=\liminf_{\substack{\varepsilon\downarrow0\\ U\ni y\to z}}u_\varepsilon(y):=\sup_{\delta>0}\ \inf\bigl\{u_\varepsilon(y):0<\varepsilon<\delta,\ y\in U,\ |y-z|<\delta\bigr\}.$$
The quantifiers range over the index $\varepsilon$ and the point $y$
simultaneously, so the limit records the behaviour of the whole family near
$z$, not the limit of the single family of values $(u_\varepsilon(z))_{\varepsilon}$;
both envelopes are local and depend only on the germ of the family at $z$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the exact finite-control coefficient hypotheses of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], in any dimension
$d\ge1$. Let $u$ be bounded upper semicontinuous and $v$ bounded lower
semicontinuous on $\mathbb T^d\times(0,T)$; assume their interior
$C^{1,2}$-test inequalities are those of
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]], using the local
maximum/minimum contact convention of
[[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]. Suppose the raw relaxed initial
traces are ordered at every $x\in\mathbb T^d$:
$$\limsup_{\substack{(y,t)\to(x,0)\\t>0}}u(y,t)\le\liminf_{\substack{(y,t)\to(x,0)\\t>0}}v(y,t).$$
Then $u\le v$ on $\mathbb T^d\times(0,T)$. In particular this applies to the
model's common continuous initial datum and its two relaxed initial
inequalities. Defining the values at $t=0$ by their respective raw upper and
lower envelopes gives the same order there. No continuity, spatial Lipschitz
bound, or differentiability of $u,v$ is assumed.

For a sequence of diagonal-diffusion grid schemes satisfying the hypotheses
of [[thm-na-diagonal-diffusion-scheme-half-relaxed-limits]], suppose in
addition that the exact periodic Cauchy problem
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] has a comparison
principle for bounded upper semicontinuous subsolutions and bounded lower
semicontinuous supersolutions with ordered relaxed initial traces. Then the
upper and lower half-relaxed limits coincide, define the unique bounded
continuous viscosity solution, and the spatially interpolated numerical
solutions converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$ to it.
This corollary is conditional on the stated second-order comparison property;
it does not supply or assert that property.

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

Use the model of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] and a periodic grid with integers $N_j\ge3$, $h_j=1/N_j$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$, set $\tau=T/M$, and put $t_n=n\tau$ for $n=0,\ldots,M$. For a nodal array $V$, define
$$D_{jj}^hV_i=\frac{V_{i+e_j}-2V_i+V_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$
For a control $a$, define
$$D_{j,a}^{up}V_i=\begin{cases}(V_i-V_{i-e_j})/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)\ge0,\\(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)/h_j,&b_j^a(x_i,t_n)<0.\end{cases}$$
The recurrence is
$$U_i^{n+1}=U_i^n+\tau\max_{a\in A}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^d\left[\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{jj}^hU_i+b_j^a(x_i,t_n)D_{j,a}^{up}U_i\right]+f^a(x_i,t_n)\right\}.$$
At each time level $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, admit the update only when, at every node, control, and coordinate,
$$|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|h_j\le\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n),$$
and
$$\tau\max_{i,a}\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{2\alpha_j^a(x_i,t_n)}{h_j^2}+\frac{|b_j^a(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\right)\le1.$$
Initialize by $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and perform the updates for $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, evaluating coefficients at $(x_i,t_n)$. Return $U^M$. No claim about an arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is included.

Identify integers and naturals with their canonical copies in the reals. For every real $x$, put $\lceil x\rceil=-\lfloor-x\rfloor$, using [[lem-integer-part]]. Then $\lceil x\rceil$ is an integer, $x\le\lceil x\rceil$, and
$$\lceil x\rceil\le m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
For $a\ge0$, the least positive integer $n$ with $n\ge a$ is $\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}$. In particular $\lceil0\rceil=0$, and $\lceil k\rceil=k$ for every integer $k$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the given mesh family. Comparison [F2] applies, because [F1] supplies exactly its bounded USC/LSC functions, interior viscosity inequalities and ordered relaxed initial traces. It gives $\overline U\le\underline U$, hence equality by the reverse inequality in [F1]. The conditional implication [F3] now has its premise proved locally, and gives the claimed bounded continuous viscosity solution and convergence on each compact cylinder $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T']$, $T'<T$. Comparing any two bounded continuous solutions in both orders using [F2] proves uniqueness. Full AC is inherited from [F2], and also supplies the Countable Choice used by [F1].

To ensure the existence conclusion is nonvacuous, choose uniform grids $N_{k,j}=N_0+k$ for every $j$, where $$N_0=\max\{3,\lceil B^*/\alpha_*\rceil\}$$ is an integer by [F5]. Put $N=N_0+k$ and $$M_k=\max\{1,\lceil T d(2A^*N^2+B^*N)\rceil\}+k,\qquad\tau_k=T/M_k.$$ Then $|b_j^a|h_j\le B^*/N\le\alpha_*\le\alpha_j^a$, while $$\tau_k\sum_j(2\alpha_j^a/h_j^2+|b_j^a|/h_j)\le (T/M_k)d(2A^*N^2+B^*N)\le1.$$ Thus every row is admissible, $h_{k,j}\to0$, and $\tau_k\le T/k\to0$. The finite recurrence in [F4] produces the numerical arrays on this explicit mesh family. Step 1.1 gives their limit and therefore existence for every stated datum and coefficient family.
